title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
On the SBE gap, you wrote:

"We believe that it is appropriate at this time to continue to exclude issuers on the State-based Exchanges (SBEs), including SBE-FPs, as impacted payers...As we assess the effectiveness of interoperability policies, we will consider whether future rulemaking to include those types of issuers as impacted payers is appropriate."

CMS needs to pick a lane here. If you have the authority to extend these requirements to state-based exchanges, extend them. If you don't, say so explicitly and tell Congress what statutory change is needed to close the gap. What we've gotten instead is three consecutive rulemakings where CMS acknowledges the coverage gap, "encourages" SBEs to consider adopting similar requirements voluntarily, solicits comment on whether to maybe do something about it next time, and moves on to the next section of the preamble.

Here are the levers CMS could pull:

For SBE-FPs (3 states) - These exchanges use HealthCare.gov for enrollment but handle their own QHP certification. CMS could condition continued access to the Federal platform (the Data Services Hub, eligibility services) on meeting interoperability requirements. The QHP Issuer Agreement that SBE-FP issuers sign with CMS already memorializes duties and obligations. Adding interoperability attestation to that agreement would be straightforward.

For fully independent SBEs (21 states): Undoubtedly harder, as CMS doesn't certify those QHPs. But you have a few options:
- ACA Section 1311 essential health benefits and certification standards give the Secretary authority to set minimum QHP certification criteria. CMS could argue interoperability requirements are a condition of QHP status, period, regardless of which exchange certifies the plan.
- Condition federal financial assistance (premium tax credits, CSR payments) on issuer compliance with interoperability requirements. If your plan doesn't support Patient Access API, your enrollees don't get subsidies.

The ~7 million Americans enrolled through SBEs deserve the same interoperability protections as everyone else. Stop teasing us. Carpe that diem and just do it already.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
The ALS Association appreciates the opportunity to comment on CMS’s proposed rule to modernize prior authorization (PA) and interoperability requirements, including the extension of these requirements to prescription drugs.

Our mission is to make ALS livable until it is cured by advancing research, supporting people living with ALS with innovative equipment and services, and advocating for policies that ensure timely access to high quality care.

The ALS Association commends CMS for prioritizing prior authorization reform and recognizing the significant impact that streamlined and modernized processes can have on patient outcomes and provider efficiency. By addressing longstanding administrative burdens and avoidable delays, CMS demonstrates a meaningful commitment to strengthening the health care system for individuals with complex medical needs, including people living with ALS. These reforms better equip providers to deliver timely, coordinated care and reduce barriers that undermine access to treatment and quality of life.

Timely access to care is essential for people living with ALS, a rapidly progressive disease that requires prompt and uninterrupted medical intervention. Delays in authorizing medically necessary services, equipment, or medications can result in irreversible loss of function, increased caregiver burden, and avoidable health complications. Prior authorization policies must therefore be designed to facilitate—rather than impede—access to the care and supports that enable individuals with ALS to maintain independence and manage symptoms effectively.

CMS has an important opportunity to ensure that prior authorization functions as a tool for appropriate care management rather than an obstacle to medically necessary treatment. Continued investment in electronic prior authorization and interoperability can reduce duplicative paperwork, expedite decision‑making, and improve communication between providers and plans. These improvements are particularly critical for ALS care, where clinical needs are urgent, ongoing, and best addressed through coordinated specialty care.

The ALS Association urges CMS to finalize this rule with strong, enforceable protections to safeguard timely and nondiscriminatory access to care. This includes adopting default expedited pathways for ALS‑related services, shortening decision timelines for urgent requests, and supporting utilization management approaches—such as appropriately structured gold‑carding programs—that recognize established provider expertise. Together, these reforms will reduce treatment disruptions, promote effective care coordination, and align utilization management with the realities of progressive and life‑limiting conditions.

In closing, the ALS Association strongly supports CMS’s efforts to modernize prior authorization and urges continued improvements that prioritize access, efficiency, and equity for medically complex patients. By implementing these reforms, CMS can strengthen the health care system’s ability to serve individuals with critical medical needs, improve the delivery of ALS care, and ensure that coverage policies support timely, patient centered treatment. We sincerely appreciate CMS’s dedication to addressing the unique challenges faced by people living with ALS and recognizing their urgent healthcare needs.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Re: CMS-0062-P, 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule
I am the CTO and co-founder of EasyPA.ai, an AI-powered prior authorization platform serving medical practices. We work daily across EMRs, clearinghouses, and payers to automate prior authorization workflows. The proposals in CMS-0062-P will materially change the infrastructure our customers and partners operate on, so I want to share field perspective on what will work, what will struggle, and what CMS can do to make this rule succeed.
Overall support
EasyPA.ai strongly supports the direction of this rule. Extending electronic prior authorization to drugs, adopting FHIR for HIPAA-covered PA transactions, aligning decision timeframes, and requiring specific reasons for denial are the right calls. They reduce burden on providers, improve patient access, and create the structured data foundation needed for trustworthy automation downstream.
HL7v2 is not going away by October 1, 2027
CMS should plan for a hybrid reality. HL7v2 still moves the majority of clinical messages between EMRs, hospitals, labs, and pharmacies in the United States today. FHIR adoption is real and accelerating, but smaller payers, rural providers, regional plans, and many state Medicaid systems will not have rebuilt their cores in the next 17 months. They will depend on bridge infrastructure that translates between HL7v2 and FHIR in both directions.
We recommend CMS explicitly acknowledge bidirectional HL7v2 to FHIR conversion as a compliant pathway, provided the FHIR endpoint exposed to trading partners conforms to the required implementation guides. Without this, smaller plans and rural providers will face binary outcomes: full rip-and-replace, or fall out of compliance. Neither serves patients.
Specific reason for denial: require structured codes, not free text
The requirement to provide a specific reason for denying drug PA requests is one of the most important provisions in this rule. To make it actually useful for providers and patients, CMS should require denial reasons to be expressed using structured FHIR coded values, not free-text strings. Free text cannot be reliably parsed for appeals, automated resubmission, or population-level analysis. Structured denial reasons unlock all three and create the data exhaust CMS itself will need to evaluate whether this rule is working.
CDex attachments: preserve flexibility, push for structured exchange where possible
Real-world PA submissions still lean heavily on PDFs, scanned documents, and faxed clinical notes. Adopting the Da Vinci CDex IG is the right move because it preserves that flexibility while creating a clean envelope. We support this. We also encourage CMS to push payers to publish, in machine-readable form, exactly which data elements they require for each PA scenario, so providers stop sending entire charts to cover unknown payer requirements.
Response to RFI on payer API implementation
API compliance is uneven today. Many published FHIR endpoints fail in production on issues that basic conformance testing would catch. CMS should require end-to-end testing against published test scripts, with results filed annually alongside the API usage metrics already proposed in this rule. Self-attestation alone has not produced reliable interoperability and will not produce it for drug PA either.
On AI in the prior authorization pipeline
CMS will receive many comments invoking artificial intelligence. The technical reality is that different AI systems do very different things in this workflow. Classification models triage and route. Generative models draft appeals and summarize clinical documentation. These are distinct capabilities with distinct risk profiles. Any future rulemaking on AI in prior authorization should make this distinction explicit and require transparency on which model types are used at each decision point, particularly when AI contributes to a denial.
Closing
The October 1, 2027 compliance date is achievable for payers that begin work now and that can access interoperability infrastructure built on open standards. EasyPA.ai is committed to supporting that transition through purpose-built tooling, including our HL7v2 to FHIR converter available on AWS Marketplace.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Respectfully,
Alex Vega
CTO, EasyPA.ai

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
CMS is proposing a rule to improve the exchange and use of health information, streamline prior authorization processes, and support continuity of care when patients switch health plans. I support this proposed rule because it has the potential to reduce administrative burdens on both patients and healthcare providers. By improving the efficiency of information sharing, the rule could help patients receive timely care and help providers spend less time navigating complex authorization requirements.

If patient information does not transfer smoothly when a person changes health plans, the patient may lose timely access to medically necessary medications or treatments. Improved data sharing and interoperability can help ensure that a patient's medical history, prior authorizations, and treatment information are available when coverage changes. This can reduce disruptions in care and help patients continue receiving appropriate treatment without unnecessary delays.

Improved sharing of health information between healthcare providers and health plans could help providers make more informed decisions more quickly. When relevant patient information is available through interoperable systems, providers may spend less time requesting records or clarifying coverage requirements. This can reduce administrative burdens, improve efficiency, and allow healthcare professionals to focus more of their time on patient care.

I believe this proposed rule will provide meaningful benefits to patients, healthcare providers, and health plans. By streamlining the exchange of health information and supporting continuity of care, the rule has the potential to improve healthcare delivery and produce positive outcomes for communities. I encourage CMS to move forward with the proposed rule.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am a practicing GYN oncologist and would like to express support for the proposed rule to improve the electronic prior authorization processes.

Patients with cancer frequently require urgent access to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapies, supportive medications, imaging studies, genetic testing, and procedures. The current prior authorization process is often fragmented, time-consuming, and administratively burdensome for both patients and providers. Delays in authorization can postpone treatment initiation, interrupt ongoing therapy, increase patient anxiety, and consume significant clinical resources that could otherwise be directed toward patient care. Practices often hire dedicated personnel to manage prior authorizations and any policy that reduces this burden allows resources to be redirected toward patient care instead of administrative tasks.

I strongly support efforts to standardize and automate prior authorization workflows. I would also encourage CMS to prioritize oncology treatments, imaging, and supportive care medications when evaluating the impact of these policies. In oncology, delays of days or weeks can have significant clinical consequences. Prior authorization systems should support timely evidence-based treatment rather than create barriers to care.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Hello Everyone

My name is Cody Adams, and I am a Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) student at Pennsylvania Western University and a nurse leader with experience in healthcare administration, quality improvement, and direct patient care. I am interested in CMS-0062-P because prior authorization requirements significantly affect patient access to medications and create administrative burdens for healthcare providers. Throughout my nursing career, I have observed treatment delays caused by prior authorization requirements and the challenges faced by clinicians attempting to obtain timely approvals for medically necessary therapies.

Background

My comments focus on CMS’s proposal requiring impacted payers to implement electronic prior authorization (ePA) for prescription drugs using standardized interoperability requirements and National Council for Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) standards. The proposed rule seeks to replace inefficient manual processes, such as fax and telephone communications, with standardized electronic exchanges that improve communication among providers, pharmacies, and health plans.

Analysis

I support the proposed rule because prior authorization remains a substantial barrier to timely healthcare delivery. According to the Medicare and Medicaid Payment and Access Commission (MACPAC, 2024), physicians and staff spend approximately 12 hours per week managing prior authorization requests. This administrative burden diverts resources away from direct patient care and contributes to provider frustration and burnout.

Patients are also negatively affected. Research by Resneck et al. (2023) found that many patients experience delays of two weeks or longer while awaiting prior authorization decisions. Such delays may interrupt treatment plans, increase patient anxiety, and potentially worsen health outcomes. These consequences are particularly concerning for patients with chronic illnesses and complex medical conditions requiring timely medication access.

The proposed electronic prior authorization requirements have the potential to improve efficiency, reduce administrative burden, and accelerate access to medications. However, electronic submission alone may not fully resolve existing challenges if payers continue requesting supplemental information outside the standardized workflow. CMS should clarify what constitutes a complete prior authorization submission and establish expectations regarding additional documentation requests.

I also believe additional transparency would strengthen the proposal. Public reporting of approval rates, denial rates, turnaround times, and common reasons for denial would improve accountability and allow stakeholders to evaluate payer performance.

Recommendations

I recommend that CMS:

Finalize the electronic prior authorization requirements and interoperability standards as proposed.
Clearly define the requirements for a complete prior authorization submission.
Require standardized electronic denial explanations that are understandable and actionable for providers.
Expand transparency through public reporting of approval rates, denial rates, turnaround times, and common denial reasons.
Provide technical assistance and implementation support for organizations with limited technological resources.
Monitor patient-centered outcomes, including treatment delays, medication adherence, and patient satisfaction.
Conclusion

CMS-0062-P represents an important opportunity to modernize prior authorization processes and improve healthcare interoperability. Current prior authorization requirements create administrative burdens and delay patient access to treatment. Implementing standardized electronic prior authorization systems can improve efficiency, reduce provider workload, and enhance patient outcomes. I support the proposed rule and encourage CMS to adopt the recommendations outlined above to maximize its effectiveness and ensure meaningful improvements in patient access to care.

References

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. (2026). Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P).

Medicare and Medicaid Payment and Access Commission. (2024). Prior Authorization in Medicaid.

Resneck, J. S., Jr., et al. (2023). Patient experiences with prior authorization and impacts on access to care. JAMA Network Open, 6(10), e2339844.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

My name is Shelly H. Glenn, and I am writing as a patient advocate and lung cancer survivor to urgently request that CMS protect patients from harmful delays and denials caused by rigid prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing. As someone who works closely with oncology patients and their care teams, I see every day how critical timely access to testing is for informed, life‑saving decisions.

We commend CMS for its continued efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes. We also appreciate the opportunity to provide feedback through the Request for Information regarding the impact of prior authorization on timely patient access to medically necessary laboratory testing, as outlined in Section III.E of CMS‑0062‑P.

It is essential that CMS protect oncology patients from delays and denials tied to prior authorization requirements for medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing.

In cancer care, timing is everything. Biomarker and specialty laboratory results guide treatment selection, treatment adjustments, disease monitoring, and clinical trial eligibility. When prior authorization rules require approval before or on the exact specimen collection date, valid specimens may be delayed, rejected, or discarded—even when the patient, physician, and laboratory acted appropriately. These administrative barriers can force repeat blood draws and delay urgent cancer care.

To ensure timely access to essential testing, CMS should require health plans to:

Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected.

Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.

Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is already available.

Require expedited review for oncology‑related diagnostic and biomarker testing.

Protect patients from surprise costs when delays stem from administrative processes.

Cancer patients deserve timely access to laboratory testing so they and their clinicians can make informed, potentially life‑saving decisions without avoidable administrative obstacles.

Sincerely, Shelly Glenn, Director National Accounts - Natera, Tampa, FL

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Dear Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services,

I am a board-certified Neurologist and Headache Specialist at Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist. I treat headache disorders including migraine, cluster headache, spinal fluid pressure headache disorders, and facial pain.

The Clinical Burden of Prior Authorization on Patient Care
During clinical evaluations, I work with patients to navigate step therapy requirements that often do not align with their needs and comorbidities. Outside of clinical care, I spend several hours per day navigating the prior authorization process. A lack of transparency requires repeated modification and re-evaluation of therapeutics discussed during the patient's visit.

I have lost count of the patients I must contact to advise that a recommended therapy has been denied. Many times the "approved" step therapy alternative is not in the patient's best interest, failing to account for family planning status or prior adverse reactions. Each denial requires appeal documentation taking a minimum of 20 minutes per therapeutic. Most patients in a neurological practice are prescribed two to three therapeutics requiring prior authorization and frequently an appeal.

The Consequences of Treatment Delays
I fully support faster prior authorization decisions to prevent delays in therapeutic management. Delays in diagnosis and treatment lead to chronification of migraine. The annual conversion rate from episodic to chronic migraine is 2.5–3.0%, with inadequate acute treatment a key modifiable risk factor (Dodick DW. Lancet. 2018;391:1315-1330). Chronic migraine carries substantially higher disability, medical costs — mean annual costs of $8,243 versus $2,649 for episodic migraine — and lost work productivity (Messali A, et al. Headache. 2016;56(2):306-322; Ashina M, et al. Lancet. 2021;397:1485-1495). The International Headache Society has called for a shift from reactive treatment to proactive, early prevention to avert disease progression (Pozo-Rosich P, et al. Cephalalgia. 2025;45(10):3331024251387721).

I look forward to seeing additional health care plan transparency as well.
Opportunity to Strengthen Reform: Aligning with the American Headache Society
CMS has an opportunity to strengthen this reform by incorporating the American Headache Society (AHS) 2024 Position Statement Update, which concluded that CGRP-targeting therapies are a first-line option for migraine prevention, removing the prior recommendation that patients first try at least two classes of non-specific oral medications (Charles AC, et al. Headache. 2024;64(4):333-341). A supporting meta-analysis confirmed CGRP monoclonal antibodies are more effective than placebo with favorable tolerability versus traditional oral preventives, supporting first-line use (Robblee J, et al. Headache. 2024;64(5):547-572).

Despite this evidence, a 2026 study found that step therapy requirements mandating non-specific oral medication trials before CGRP-targeted therapies remained largely in place 10 months after the AHS statement, limiting patient access (Moskatel LS, Slusky DJG. Headache. 2026;66(4):801-812).

I recommend that CMS require health plans to align prior authorization and step therapy criteria with the AHS 2024 Position Statement, permitting CGRP medications for both prevention and acute management of migraine as first-line options without mandating failure of non-specific oral medications first.

Respectfully submitted,

Barbara L. Nye MD
Board-Certified Neurologist and Headache Medicine Specialist
Atrium Health
Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center
Department of Neurology

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment: I am a headache specialist in New York City that treats headache disorder patients daily. In my practice I have experienced the effect of prior sighs and step therapy on my patients. Routinely I’ve had patients care be delayed with prolonged debilitation due to waiting for prior authorization. One example i would like to highlight is a young 31 year old who has had to leave her job that she loves because of uncontrolled migraine headaches. Ideally I’d like to get her on CGRP injectable medications which is recommended and recognized as a first line treatment for migraine headaches as put out by the public statement from the American Headache Society. However we’ve had to trial multiple step therapies that she’s been unresponsive to and had terrible side effects for over the last year in order to fail step therapy to get to CGRPs. The current proposal to expedite prior authorization time is amazing, and will help move treatment forward but progressing treatment coverage would also decrease debilitation time and years for patients, lower ER visits and burden on the system.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am a physician, neurologist, headache specialist, and a person living with migraine with aura. I agree with recommendations to shorten times for prior authorization determinations and to eliminate as many barriers as possible to step therapy requirements for medications.

Migraine is a chronic neurologic disease that is the number one leading cause of disability for women under 50 and one of the top five leading causes of years lived with disability globally. I have had multiple patients present to me specify when asked how many hours of their lives they have lost to migraine, they will specify years worth of hours and days spent on the couch or in bed, disabled by migraine. Multiple individuals within my practice alone have lost their jobs to migraine.

Prior authorizations cause a significant delay in providing medical care for patients when delayed. These hours, days, weeks and even months of delay can worsen a patient's ability to work and sometimes those instances will make the difference between working to getting fired and losing their jobs. Multiple patients have repeatedly stated that because of step therapy requirements, they have spent months or years battling insurance to get on recommended, targeted medical therapies.

In my practice, prior authorization delays additional cause significant administrative burden on our staff. I agree that faster decisions, less requirements for patients to getting into medical therapies, forced switches based on insurance formularies and not on patients prior clinical responses or medical necessity would vastly improve patients' quality of life and overall medical expenditures.

The American headache society in 2024 recommended cgrp migraine targeted treatment options as preventive first line medical therapies in migraine and for rescue therapies these are immensely important and effective when used as first line therapies. CMS should consider this when deciding on future rules and formulary requirements/precedent moving forward.

Often times, prior authorizations are not clear what they require from an office on how patients can start therapies, or the requirements necessary do not make sense or are contraindicated for patients. Electronic prior authorization status updates should be required as insurances often will not answer requests for feedback or provide clear updates. Overall, patients need expedited access to care that is medically recommended by their providers.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
The Denial Reason Requirement Must Distinguish Substantive from Procedural Denials:
As currently proposed, the rule requires payers to provide "a specific reason" for drug PA denials. This is an important step forward, but the rule does not define what qualifies as a specific reason or require payers to distinguish between fundamentally different types of denials - the difference between a transparency requirement with teeth and one that legitimizes harmful payer behavior in more legible language.

Denials fall into two distinct categories. Procedural denials are issued when a request fails administrative or formulary requirements; they reflect administrative criteria, not clinical judgment. Substantive denials are issued when a payer determines a drug is not medically necessary; a clinical judgment made without examining the patient and without accountability for the outcome.

The proposed rule treats these identically. A payer satisfies the "specific reason" requirement by stating "step therapy requirements not met" -- telling a provider nothing about whether the patient's history was reviewed, prior treatment failures considered, or a medical necessity exception even exists. For individuals with serious mental illness, this distinction is not semantic; it is clinical.

We urge CMS to amend the denial reason requirement to require: mandatory categorization of denials as procedural or substantive (defined in regulation); clinical basis disclosure for substantive denials; exception pathway disclosure for procedural denials, identifying the override process and timeframe; and a prohibition on characterizing medical necessity determinations as procedural denials.

For antipsychotics specifically, step therapy denials are routinely issued as procedural matters when the payer has made a clinical determination that the prescribed medication is unnecessary. That determination is wrong, it is harmful, and the proposed rule does not yet require payers to make it visible.

Existing Antipsychotic Protections Are Real but Critically Incomplete

Antipsychotics are one of six protected drug classes under Medicare Part D, a protection we acknowledge. However, the existing framework contains significant structural gaps that leave large portions of this population exposed to harmful step therapy, gaps this proposed rule has the opportunity to close.

Under Part D, plans must include all antipsychotics on formularies and may not apply step therapy to patients already established on therapy. This is meaningful, but it has critical limits.

Gap 1: New patients on Part D are not protected. The policy permits step therapy for new starts - meaning a patient newly diagnosed with schizophrenia, or new to a plan, can face step therapy before accessing the medication their psychiatrist prescribed. Early treatment decisions in psychotic illness are among the most consequential - a failed medication trial can trigger relapse from which recovery is uncertain. This is not a technicality; it is a clinical vulnerability.

Gap 2: Injectable antipsychotics under Part B are not protected at all. The protected class policy does not apply to Medicare Part B, which covers long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics - critical for individuals who struggle with oral adherence. Medicare Advantage plans may apply step therapy to LAIs without Part D safeguards. For many individuals with severe psychotic illness, LAIs are not a preference. They are a clinical necessity.

Gap 3: Existing protections are under active pressure. Cost-containment initiatives like the GUARD model risk eroding these protections. The protected class framework requires active defense and this rulemaking is an opportunity to strengthen it.

Antipsychotic medications are not interchangeable, supported by decades of evidence, and we urge CMS to recognize:

Psychiatric medication switches carry serious, sometimes irreversible risks. Each switch carries risk of relapse, hospitalization, and functional deterioration, including neurological changes that can make future treatment less effective. Forcing a patient off a stable regimen to satisfy a formulary preference is a clinical intervention made without physician judgment or accountability for the outcome.

There is no "equivalent" antipsychotic. These medications differ substantially in mechanism of action, side effect profiles, delivery method, and individual response. What stabilizes one patient may destabilize another. Step therapy protocols that treat antipsychotics as interchangeable are not evidence-based; they are cost-driven, and the costs shifted onto patients are human ones.

The consequences extend beyond the individual. Forced medication switches drive emergency visits, hospitalizations, criminal justice involvement, and family crisis - downstream costs that far exceed any short-term formulary savings. CMS has visibility into this data, and the pattern is consistent and clear.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
CMS-0062-P — 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing in strong support of CMS’s proposed efforts to improve prior authorization transparency, interoperability, and timeliness under CMS-0062-P. As a practicing psychiatrist and medical leader involved in treating patients with severe and treatment-resistant psychiatric illness, I believe these reforms are critically needed—particularly for advanced psychiatric treatments such as Spravato (esketamine) and Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).

Patients who qualify for Spravato or TMS often suffer from treatment-resistant depression, severe suicidal ideation, obsessive-compulsive disorder, or other highly impairing psychiatric conditions. These individuals have frequently failed multiple traditional medication trials and may be experiencing substantial functional decline, hospitalization risk, suicidality, inability to work, or profound impairment in daily living. Delays in treatment access can therefore result in serious clinical deterioration, psychiatric hospitalization, emergency department utilization, self-harm risk, and increased healthcare costs.

Current prior authorization processes for advanced psychiatric treatments are frequently burdensome, inconsistent, duplicative, and excessively delayed. Providers are often required to repeatedly submit documentation that already clearly demonstrates medical necessity. These delays create significant administrative burden while placing vulnerable patients at substantial clinical risk.

The patients needing these treatments have already undergone extensive medication trials and psychotherapy before being considered for treatment. Yet providers commonly encounter repetitive authorization requirements, inconsistent payer criteria, and repeated requests for documentation that delay access to care. These barriers are especially concerning given the strong evidence base supporting these treatments as safe and effective treatment for treatment-resistant depression and other psychiatric disorders.

I strongly support CMS proposals that would:

• Require electronic prior authorization capabilities for drugs and medical services
• Establish standardized response timelines for prior authorizations
• Require specific reasons for denials
• Increase public reporting and transparency regarding prior authorization metrics

I also encourage CMS to consider the following additional protections and clarifications for psychiatric treatments such as Spravato and TMS:

Enforce Rapid Review Standards for Serious Psychiatric Conditions
Psychiatric illnesses can rapidly worsen when treatment is delayed. Expedited review standards should explicitly include severe treatment-resistant depression, suicidality, and other serious psychiatric conditions. Delays measured in weeks can have life-threatening consequences.
Reduce Redundant Step Therapy and Documentation Requirements
Many patients seeking Spravato or TMS have already failed multiple evidence-based treatments. Excessive or repetitive step therapy beyond established clinical guidelines unnecessarily delays medically necessary care and prolongs suffering.
Improve Transparency Around Denials
Providers should receive clinically meaningful explanations for denials, including the exact missing criteria, records, or rationale. Generic denial language creates unnecessary appeals, delays, and administrative waste.
Promote Continuity of Care
Patients who are stabilized and responding to Spravato or TMS should not face repeated interruptions due to recurring administrative barriers. Continuity of treatment is especially important in severe psychiatric illness.
Encourage Greater Standardization Across Payers
Significant variability exists among payers regarding psychiatric prior authorization criteria, particularly for TMS. Greater standardization would reduce administrative burden and improve equitable patient access to evidence-based care.
Recognize the Severity of Behavioral Health Conditions
Behavioral health conditions often carry significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and healthcare utilization. Prior authorization systems should account for the time-sensitive and medically serious nature of psychiatric care similarly to other high-risk medical conditions.

CMS’s proposed interoperability and prior authorization reforms represent an important step toward improving patient access, reducing administrative waste, and supporting timely evidence-based care. These reforms can meaningfully improve outcomes for patients suffering from severe mental illness while reducing downstream healthcare costs associated with untreated or undertreated psychiatric disease.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important proposed rule.

Sincerely,

Thomas Rayner, MD
Chief Medical Officer
Whole Mind

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
As a healthcare leader responsible for clinical informatics and operational workflows, I strongly support the intent of this proposed rule to modernize prior authorization through improved interoperability and electronic processes. Prior authorization delays are not simply administrative inefficiencies—they directly impact patient care. When approvals are delayed, patients experience postponed treatments, interruptions in medication access, and, in some cases, worsening clinical outcomes. For this reason, the proposed decision timeframes are not just operational benchmarks; they are critical patient safety safeguards. However, the effectiveness of this rule will depend on meaningful enforcement. If payers are not held accountable to consistently meet these timelines, the burden of delay will continue to fall on patients despite the transition to electronic systems.
Additionally, it is essential that payers bear the primary responsibility for the costs and operational lift associated with integration and implementation. Prior authorization requirements originate from payer policies, and the administrative complexity that this rule seeks to address has largely been driven by payer processes. While providers will need to interact with enhanced digital workflows, shifting the cost burden onto health systems would further strain organizations already managing significant clinical and financial pressures. True reform requires clear accountability—both in terms of adherence to required timelines and investment in the infrastructure needed to support interoperability. Without enforceable standards and appropriate allocation of responsibility, there is a risk that these changes will not achieve their intended impact. Ensuring payer accountability will be key to delivering meaningful improvements in efficiency, transparency, and, most importantly, patient care.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am submitting this comment as a prior authorization and FHIR interoperability consultant with direct experience supporting payers, providers, and health-tech teams navigating CMS interoperability requirements and Da Vinci implementation work.
I support the core objective of CMS-0062-P — extending electronic prior authorization requirements to drugs and shortening decision timeframes. The operational case for this direction is well-established. Manual drug prior authorization workflows create avoidable delays in medication access, drive unnecessary administrative burden, and produce inconsistent denial rationale that makes appeals difficult for providers and patients alike. Extending the electronic prior authorization framework to drugs is the right direction.
However I want to offer operationally grounded comments on three specific aspects of the proposed rule that I believe require further consideration before finalization.
DECISION TIMEFRAME FEASIBILITY
The proposed compression of standard drug prior authorization decisions to 72 hours and urgent decisions to 24 hours is significantly more aggressive than the current non-drug PA requirements. I support shorter timeframes as a goal. My concern is sequencing. Organizations that have not yet completed workflow redesign for non-drug PA — which represents a substantial portion of affected payers — will face compounded implementation pressure. I recommend CMS consider a phased approach that allows payers to demonstrate operational readiness at the non-drug PA standard before the drug PA timeframes take effect. Compliance with a timeline that outpaces operational capacity produces paper compliance, not genuine improvement in patient access.
WORKFLOW DESIGN BEFORE API REQUIREMENT
The most significant implementation failure pattern I observe across prior authorization modernization efforts is the assumption that API compliance produces operational results. It does not. A FHIR Prior Authorization API built on top of broken intake, documentation, routing, and status workflows produces a compliant system that still delivers poor operational performance. I urge CMS to strengthen guidance around workflow readiness requirements alongside the technical API specifications — specifically around intake completeness, documentation alignment, and denial rationale generation. Technical conformance testing through Inferno validates API endpoints. It does not validate that those endpoints are connected to workflows capable of meeting the proposed decision timeframes.
HUMAN ACCOUNTABILITY IN AI-ASSISTED DRUG PA
As AI-assisted prior authorization tools are increasingly deployed to support the shorter decision timeframes this rule proposes, I urge CMS to strengthen its guidance on human accountability requirements for drug PA decisions. Drug prior authorization decisions directly affect patient access to medication — with immediate health consequences when delays occur. ONC's HTI-1 Final Rule is establishing algorithm transparency requirements for AI in certified health IT. CMS-0062-P should explicitly align with that direction by requiring that AI-assisted drug PA workflows maintain documented human accountability at the decision point. Automated denial of a drug prior authorization request without human review creates both patient safety risk and compliance exposure that the proposed rule should address directly.
I appreciate CMS's continued leadership on prior authorization modernization and support the overall direction of this proposed rule. The comments above are offered in the interest of ensuring that the final rule produces genuine operational improvement in patient access — not just technical compliance.
Respectfully submitted,
Pete Moses
MosesAI Consulting
Prior Authorization and FHIR Interoperability Consultant

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Calvient is a healthcare technology company that develops AI-powered solutions for prior authorizations, referrals, intelligent document processing, fax management, and healthcare operations automation. We serve federally qualified health centers (FQHCs), community health centers, and health systems across the United States.

We strongly support CMS-0062-P and the extension of electronic prior authorization requirements to prescription drugs. The compressed decision timeframes (24-hour urgent, 72-hour standard), adoption of FHIR and NCPDP standards, specific denial reason requirements, and public reporting of PA metrics are all essential reforms. Our detailed comments are provided in the attached document.

We wish to highlight one central point: the fax is not the problem. While electronic transmission standards are necessary, the true burden lies in the intensity, variability, and volume of payer-specific documentation requirements. Providers at FQHCs and health systems dedicate full-time staff solely to completing PA questionnaires, scrubbing patient charts for relevant clinical data, and monitoring submission status. Moving from fax to API makes submission faster but does not reduce this preparatory work.

This is why the Da Vinci Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR) implementation guide is the most consequential element of this rule. DTR enables payers to deliver documentation requirements in structured, machine-readable formats that can be pre-populated with clinical data from the patient record. We urge CMS to mandate DTR adoption with the same urgency as PAS.

We also urge CMS to recognize the emerging role of AI-augmented workflows in prior authorization. AI agents are already assisting providers by scrubbing charts, pre-populating questionnaire responses, verifying PA necessity, and monitoring submission status. These tools do not replace human clinical judgment, but rather augment human capabilities and efficiency. The EPA framework established by this rule should be designed to facilitate AI-assisted workflows by ensuring DTR questionnaires are machine-processable, PAS APIs support programmatic status queries, and payer API access policies accommodate technology-assisted throughput.

Our attached comment provides detailed recommendations including: mandating DTR with equal urgency to PAS, requiring PA necessity determination via API, establishing questionnaire consistency standards, designing EPA for AI-augmented workflows, and addressing the unique needs of FQHCs. We also respond to the RFIs on step therapy, laboratory/DME PA burden, and cybersecurity.

Calvient welcomes the opportunity to serve as a resource to CMS on this rulemaking.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
PUBLIC COMMENT ON CMS-0062-P
Docket: CMS-2026-1255-0001
RFI Addressed: III.C. Improving Implementation of Payer API Technology
Submitted by: Akken Yakupitiyage, Founder, Zkeleton

This is a summary. The full comment is in the attached PDF.

I am the founder of Zkeleton, a pre-seed company building clinical data normalization infrastructure for health plans. Zkeleton is not a regulated entity under this rule, does not currently sell into the impacted payer categories, and has no direct commercial position in the outcome.

The proposed rule meaningfully advances interoperability by extending API requirements to drugs and establishing an endpoint registry. The most important unaddressed risk is the gap between technical conformance to FHIR implementation guides and the practical usability of the data those guides convey.

THE CONFORMANCE GAP

Conformance ensures that data moves. Fidelity ensures that data arrives in a form the receiving payer can act on. The current testing framework, including ONC Inferno, validates the first but not the second. Five patterns illustrate the gap:

1. Unstructured attachments under CDex. Two payers can pass conformance while one transmits structured Observations with LOINC codes and the other transmits a scanned PDF of the same lab.

2. Code system fragmentation. Prior treatment history may appear as RxNorm RXCUIs, NDCs, internal payer codes, or free text. All conformant; only the first supports automated decisioning.

3. Semantic loss across Payer-to-Payer. A member who cleared step therapy at one payer may be forced to repeat it at the next, because the receiving payer cannot operationalize the prior failure history even though it was technically transmitted.

4. Absence of round-trip scenario testing. No widely adopted test verifies that a clinically meaningful PA scenario can be transmitted, received, and rendered into a coverage decision without semantic loss.

5. Identity and demographic resolution. Patient matching across payers is governed by each payer's internal algorithms, with no rule-level expectations for matching quality or transparency.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Establish semantic fidelity benchmarks alongside conformance testing, covering structured-Observation rates, RxNorm-encoding rates, and structured-rationale rates for PA decisions. Publishing them is itself a market signal.

2. Require structured representation when the source representation is structured. PDF wrapping of natively structured data should be discouraged through the testing and certification framework.

3. Develop a reference test corpus for round-trip scenarios covering specialty drugs with prior step therapy, oncology with biomarker-based eligibility, transplant immunosuppressants, and autoimmune biologics.

4. Publish a data fidelity score alongside the API endpoint registry described in Section II.E, so receiving payers, providers, and patients can assess upstream quality and payers have a market incentive to invest in fidelity.

5. Clarify that nothing in the conformance and testing framework prohibits payers from staging, normalizing, or quality-checking ingested clinical data in segregated or single-tenant processing environments before promoting it to operational systems. This clarification removes ambiguity for payer privacy, security, and compliance teams considering modern data architectures.

TRADEOFFS

Three tradeoffs are worth naming. First, fidelity benchmarks add cost and could slow small payer adoption; CMS should consider phasing them twelve to eighteen months after conformance compliance. Second, premature standardization is a real risk; the recommendations above are framed as benchmarks rather than fixed mandates to allow evolution. Third, burden on small entities is real and should be mitigated through delayed timelines or modified expectations for smaller payers.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR PATIENTS

The drug prior authorization extension addresses care categories where delay translates directly into harm: specialty drugs, oncology regimens, autoimmune biologics. A patient who has cleared step therapy at one plan should not be forced to repeat it at the next because the receiving payer cannot operationalize the prior failure history. Conformance moves the data. Fidelity ensures it can be used.

The attached PDF contains the full analysis of each gap and recommendation. I appreciate the opportunity to comment and would welcome follow-up from CMS staff on the technical specifics.

Respectfully submitted,

Akken Yakupitiyage
Founder, Zkeleton
akkenyaku@zkeleton.com

We support delaying the electronic prior authorization mandate for the MIPS, MSSP, and Promoting Interoperability programs until at least Performance Year 2028. A delay is necessary to allow organizations sufficient time to develop, implement, and operationalize the required infrastructure while minimizing unintended disruption to clinical workflows.

Providing clear guidance on the applicable timeframe will enable organizations to appropriately align operational, technical, and staffing resources to meet compliance expectations.

Piedmont Healthcare

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
To Whom It May Concern:
My name is Peggy Cottrell, and I am writing as a healthcare provider to urgently request that CMS protect patients from critical care delays and denials caused by rigid prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing.
As a genetic counselor working for Sharsheret, an organization representing oncology patients, we see firsthand how our callers struggle to obtain coverage for the lifesaving treatments they need.
We commend CMS for its ongoing efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes. We also deeply appreciate the opportunity to provide specific feedback via the “Request for Information regarding the impact of prior authorization on timely patient access to medically necessary laboratory testing, as referenced in Section III.E of CMS-0062-P”.
I urge CMS to protect oncology patients from delays and denials caused by prior authorization requirements for medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing.
In cancer care, timing is critical. Biomarker and specialty lab results often guide treatment selection, treatment changes, disease monitoring, and clinical trial eligibility. When prior authorization rules require approval before or on the exact specimen collection date, valid specimens may be delayed, rejected, or discarded—even when the patient, physician, and laboratory acted in good faith. This can force repeat blood draws and delay urgent cancer care.
CMS should require health plans to:
1. Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected.
2. Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.
3. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available.
4. Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.
5. Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative.
Cancer patients need timely access to laboratory testing so they and their care teams can make informed, potentially life-saving treatment decisions without unnecessary administrative barriers.
Sincerely,
Peggy Cottrell, MS, CGC
Genetics Program Manager
Sharsheret, The Jewish Breast & Ovarian Cancer Community
Teaneck, NJ

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I support CMS’s continued efforts to modernize and standardize prior authorization, particularly the expansion of electronic prior authorization (ePA) to medications. This is a critical step toward reducing administrative burden and improving access to timely care.
From a health system and clinical informatics perspective, I would highlight several considerations to ensure the rule achieves its intended impact:
1. Workflow integration must be prioritized over simple digitization.
While the proposed APIs enable electronic exchange, requiring true integration of prior authorization into EHR workflows (e.g., FHIR-based, in-context clinical decision support) is essential. Portal-based or fragmented solutions will not meaningfully reduce provider burden.
2. CMS should encourage real-time or near-real-time decisioning.
The combination of FHIR APIs and Real-Time Prescription Benefit tools creates an opportunity for point-of-care decisioning. Policies should incentivize immediate approvals where criteria are met, minimizing delays in therapy initiation.
3. Denial transparency should be actionable, not just descriptive.
In addition to requiring reason codes, CMS should require that payers provide specific, clinically relevant next steps (e.g., covered alternatives, documentation gaps, or criteria thresholds) in a structured format usable within EHR workflows.
4. Guard against unintended burden shifting to providers.
Without usability and integration standards, the operational burden may shift from manual payer workflows to provider teams navigating multiple electronic tools. CMS should consider usability expectations and provider workflow impact as part of compliance and reporting.
5. Support use of AI-enabled documentation and automation.
As health systems deploy ambient documentation and AI-assisted clinical tools, CMS should ensure that structured data generated from these tools can be used to populate and submit prior authorization requests without additional manual effort.
6. Strengthen performance measurement.
In addition to API usage, CMS should track:

Time from order to authorization decision
Time to therapy initiation
Provider time spent per authorization

These measures more directly reflect patient access and clinician burden.
Overall, this proposed rule is a strong step forward. With additional emphasis on workflow integration, real-time decisioning, and actionable transparency, CMS can significantly accelerate progress toward a fully modernized prior authorization process.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
RE: CMS-0062-P — Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule

I am writing as an individual physician in support of the CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P). I am a neurologist and headache specialist at Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, where I care for patients with migraine and other headache disorders, including a significant number of Medicare beneficiaries with chronic migraine.

I strongly support this proposed rule and write to urge CMS to strengthen its protections — particularly around repeat reauthorization, step therapy, and continuity of care for patients who are stable on effective treatment.

Prior authorization and repeat reauthorization cause direct, measurable patient harm.

In my practice, I have witnessed firsthand how prior authorization and particularly repeat reauthorization requirements disrupt care for patients who are already doing well. One patient I care for is a 68-year-old woman with chronic migraine who, before treatment, had been forced to leave her career as a nonprofit executive director due to the frequency and severity of her attacks and repeated hospitalizations. After initiating a CGRP-targeting therapy, her headache frequency and overall symptom burden decreased by more than 75%. She returned to work. She reclaimed her life.

Then her medication was delayed and ultimately denied due to burdensome repeat prior authorization requirements — despite documented, substantial clinical benefit. She was required to transition to a different medication. In the three to four months without her effective therapy, she has already visited urgent care and the emergency department twice.

This is not a billing dispute. This is a patient who was well, who is now sick again, because of an administrative process that had nothing to do with her clinical reality.

What I am asking CMS to strengthen.

First, CMS should establish meaningful protections for continuity of care. Patients who are stable on an effective therapy — particularly those with documented clinical response — should not be required to re-justify that treatment at arbitrary intervals. Repeat reauthorization for stable patients on proven therapy is medically inappropriate and causes harm.

Second, CMS should address step therapy. Fail-first requirements force patients to try medications that may be contraindicated, previously failed, or medically inappropriate before accessing the treatment their clinician has determined is right for them. This delays effective care, prolongs disability, and in the case of migraine, can contribute to the progression from episodic to chronic disease — a progression that is far harder to reverse than it is to prevent.

Third, coverage criteria should reflect current evidence-based clinical guidelines. The American Headache Society and the American Academy of Neurology have established clinical guidance on appropriate migraine treatment. Insurance coverage criteria should align with — not contradict — these standards.

In summary, patient I described above is not an outlier. She is one of many patients in my practice and across the country whose care has been disrupted not by the limits of medicine, but by the limits of administrative systems that were not designed with their wellbeing in mind.

CMS has an opportunity to change that with this rule. I urge you to finalize it with strong, enforceable protections for continuity of care, meaningful step therapy reform, and coverage criteria grounded in current clinical evidence.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully,

Amaal J. Starling, MD, FAHS, FAAN
Associate Professor of Neurology
Program Director, Transitional Year Residency
Department of Neurology
Mayo Clinic
13400 East Shea Boulevard
Scottsdale, Arizona 85259

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am a Physician Assistant specializing in neurology. Every single day, I work on the front lines of patient care, diagnosing and treating complex neurological conditions where timely, effective intervention is critical to preserving function and patient quality of life. The current administrative burdens imposed by insurers severely disrupt evidence-based medical care.Impact of Prior Authorization Delays: Prior authorization (PA) protocols create unnecessary bottlenecks that delay crucial treatments for weeks or months. In neurology, where conditions like progressive multiple sclerosis, intractable epilepsy, or chronic migraines require rapid stabilization, these administrative delays cause preventable disease progression and prolonged patient suffering. Forcing patients to undergo "fail-first" protocols ignores evidence-based clinical guidelines. Patients are routinely required to trial and fail older, less effective, or less tolerable medications before gaining access to the therapies originally prescribed. This process is highly burdensome, causes unnecessary adverse side effects, and strips patients of their autonomy.

Critical, complex therapies administered directly in the clinic—such as therapeutic botulinum toxin injections or specialized intravenous infusions—are frequently delayed by fragmented medical benefit approval processes. This forces patients to miss essential dosing windows.
Insurers frequently alter formulary coverages and PA rules mid-year without providing sufficient advance notice to clinicians or patients. This lack of transparency leads to sudden medication disruptions at the pharmacy counter, forcing stable patients into unexpected step therapy cycles or sudden denials.A Specific Clinical ExampleI recently treated a patient suffering from severe chronic migraines who met all evidence-based criteria for a targeted, modern CGRP inhibitor. Instead of approving the medication, the insurance provider mandated a step therapy protocol requiring the patient to try and "fail" two older generic alternatives first. The forced trial of these less tolerable options caused the patient severe fatigue and cognitive slowing—profoundly impacting their ability to work. By the time we navigated the paperwork and successive denials, the patient was completely demoralized. This unnecessary cycle caused them to lose trust in the medical system—and ultimately in medicine altogether.
I strongly support the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) ⁠2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule. Specifically, I commend the following provisions:Faster Decisions: Shortening the mandated timeframes for PA determinations is a vital step toward protecting patient health and reducing treatment gaps.Expanded Electronic Prior Authorization (e-PA): Requiring payers to support standardized Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) for all drugs will drastically minimize the manual faxing and phone calls that drain clinic resources.Health Plan Transparency: Forcing payers to publicly report aggregate PA metrics—including specific reasons for denials—will finally hold insurance companies accountable for arbitrary coverage roadblocks.What CMS Should StrengthenWhile the proposed rule is an excellent foundation, CMS must go further to protect vulnerable patients. I strongly urge CMS to incorporate the position statements and recommendations of specialty groups like the ⁠American Headache Society (AHS) to solidify these reforms:Streamline and Restrict Step Therapy: CMS must use its oversight to explicitly prohibit insurers from requiring step therapy when a clinician provides documented evidence that the preferred tier-one drug is clinically inappropriate or carries a high risk of adverse effects.Protect Stable Patients: Implement strict grandfathering clauses. A patient who is clinically stable on a medication must never be forced into a "fail-first" step therapy protocol due to a mid-year formulary change or an insurance switch.Standardize Peer-to-Peer Reviews: CMS should mandate that any specialized neurological PA denial be reviewed exclusively by a board-certified neurologist or a peer with direct expertise in the specific neurological condition, rather than a general reviewer.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment: That prior authorization requires severe reform can be seen from even a cursory overview of its public-facing process.  Requirements for authorization of tests or treatments are not standardized even within a specific insurance company, differing from one plan to the next.  It’s impossible to know or look up criteria for innumerable tests and treatments.  Companies use phone-tree and call center gatekeepers who shield decision-makers from being contacted.  Documentation is burdensome and done by cumbersome faxing.  When portals exist, they are clunky and difficult to use, and the physician, who may lack authority to sign a contract within an organization, is forced to sign one in order to get access.  Denials are algorithmic and automatic in many cases, such that appeal is the only way to seek approval, putting massive stress on physicians and nurses, and inevitably delaying the process.  Reviewers are not of the same specialty as the requesting physician, and reviews aren’t substantive, as the reviewers are required to restrict their opinions to plan language not the best interests of the patient.  Every time Earth circles the Sun, the annual review puts the patient at risk for interruption of therapy.  There’s no way for physicians to speak with anyone who has decision making authority, even upon urgent demand.  The structure of the prior authorization system alone is diagnostic of a bad faith process.  One doesn’t even have to delve into the details of what’s covered and what’s not in order to expose prior authorization as a crude process designed to deter medical care, and to undo whatever a physician has already done.  It’s not even necessary to recount the harms done to patients by this process to know that it’s a heartless cost control mechanism.  This is my personal opinion, not that of any organization.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Re: CMS-0062-P; 91 FR 19890; RIN 0938-AV44

CMS's proposed HL7 FHIR-based prior authorization requirements and NCPDP pharmacy standards create a meaningful opportunity to improve electronic prior authorization for drugs covered under medical and pharmacy benefits. One useful addition to the final rule would be an operational performance layer that helps CMS assess whether interoperability conformance translates into usable workflows for prescribers, pharmacies, care teams, and patients after go-live. API availability, usage reporting, denial-reason fields, CRD/DTR/PAS implementation, NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary & Benefit, and Real-Time Prescription Benefit standards are important technical measures. Adoption and burden-reduction metrics would give CMS a clearer way to evaluate whether implementation reduces manual workarounds, improves medication-access coordination, and protects timely therapy in practice.

I support modernizing interoperability standards and prior authorization for drugs. The final rule would be stronger if CMS paired the technical requirements with seven operational safeguards:

1. Exact denial rationales that identify missing documentation, coverage criteria, medical-necessity basis, step therapy requirements, formulary restrictions, quantity limits, or clinical pathway requirements.

2. Real-time authorization status visibility across prescribers, pharmacies, patients, and care teams to reduce rework, duplicate submissions, and medication-access delays.

3. Specialty-level medication access and outcome reporting for oncology, behavioral health, specialty pharmacy, and chronic disease treatment.

4. Interoperability and pharmacy workflow burden metrics that track FHIR/NCPDP-enabled workflow performance, documentation effort, submission-to-decision time, duplicate requests, resubmissions, appeals, manual workarounds, claims disruption, medication abandonment, and provider/pharmacy workload.

5. Provider and pharmacy adoption metrics that distinguish true electronic prior authorization use from reliance on portals, fax, calls, workarounds, and duplicate documentation.

6. Implementation accountability, funding clarity, training, and adoption requirements that identify impacted payer, vendor, pharmacy, and provider responsibilities for upgrades, testing, training, dashboards, support, escalation, optimization, and sustainment.

7. Human clinical review before a denial interrupts time-sensitive therapy, triggers treatment substitution, prevents dispensing, or overrides a treating clinician's care plan.

My comments reflect more than two decades of leading enterprise health system operations and federal modernization efforts, in which interoperability standards, clinical workflows, access operations, pharmacy coordination, reimbursement integrity, user adoption, and sustainment governance had to work together at scale.

The direct obligations fall primarily on impacted payers. Prescribers, pharmacies, clinics, and health systems serving affected patients may carry a downstream burden if workflow redesign, training, upgrades, dashboards, and sustainment remain local responsibilities. CMS should clarify whether the final rule or guidance includes deployment funding, reimbursement, incentives, federal matching, vendor obligations, or technical assistance for EHR upgrades, pharmacy system changes, testing, staff training, dashboards, workflow redesign, and optimization.

The key risk is not whether interoperable electronic prior authorization for drugs can move information faster. The risk is whether impacted payers can move unresolved work back to prescribers, pharmacies, care teams, and patients while still appearing compliant. A faster denial, a vague denial, or a denial requiring repeated documentation cycles does not reduce the burden.

Successful implementation should not be defined by API availability, endpoint reporting, interoperability conformance, or transaction volume alone. CMS should define success in terms of accountable outcomes: high prescriber/pharmacy adoption, reduced portal/fax use, shorter authorization cycle time, fewer duplicative requests, fewer resubmissions and appeals, fewer dispensing delays, lower medication abandonment, clear escalation ownership, and monitoring of high-risk medication access.

CMS should not finalize CMS-0062-P until the final rule requires interoperability performance monitoring, denial specificity, status visibility, specialty-level medication-access surveillance, workflow burden reduction, adoption reporting, implementation accountability, deployment funding clarity, sustainment governance, technical assistance for lower-resource settings, and human clinical review for high-risk medication decisions.

Detailed comments are attached.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
To Whom It May Concern:
My name is Caroline Koffke, and I am writing as a patient advocate and healthcare provider to urgently request that CMS protect patients from critical care delays and denials caused by rigid prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing.
Living Beyond Breast Cancer (LBBC) is a national breast cancer non-profit that reaches around 2 million individuals each year. Many of our constituents are on either Medicare and Medicaid and depend on frequent bloodwork for the short- and long-term management of their breast cancer.
We commend CMS for its ongoing efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes. We also deeply appreciate the opportunity to provide specific feedback via the Request for Information regarding the impact of prior authorization on timely patient access to medically necessary laboratory testing, as referenced in Section III.E of CMS-0062-P.
I urge CMS to protect oncology patients from delays and denials caused by prior authorization requirements for medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing.
In cancer care, timing is critical. Biomarker and specialty lab results often guide treatment selection, treatment changes, disease monitoring, and clinical trial eligibility. When prior authorization rules require approval before or on the exact specimen collection date, valid specimens may be delayed, rejected, or discarded—even when the patient, physician, and laboratory acted in good faith. This can force repeat blood draws and delay urgent cancer care.
CMS should require health plans to:
1.Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected.
2.Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.
3.Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available.
4.Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.
5.Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative.
Cancer patients need timely access to laboratory testing so they and their care teams can make informed, potentially life-saving treatment decisions without unnecessary administrative barriers.
Sincerely,

Caroline Koffke, RN, BSN, OCN
Director, Educational and Healthcare Provider Programs
Living Beyond Breast Cancer
Bala Cynwyd, PA

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001

To: Administrator, CMS | Re: CMS-0062-P | Docket CMS-2026-1255 | From: Joanne Bayouk, MBA, MSN, RN, PMHNP | Just Care | justcare.substack.com
I submit these comments as a clinician with over 20 years spanning payer operations, PBM, utilization management, and behavioral health care delivery.
Comment 1 — BH Drugs: The GAO found CMS does not audit BH prior authorization in MA despite 8 of 9 MA organizations requiring it (GAO-25-107342, 2025). Johns Hopkins found PA linked to treatment interruptions, relapse, and worse outcomes in behavioral health (Murphy et al., 2026). CMS must confirm psychiatric and SUD medications are covered, expedited timelines apply for acute BH need, and payers cannot impose more restrictive standards than comparable medical drug classes under MHPAEA.
Comment 2 — FHIR Criteria: Mandating FHIR data exchange while permitting proprietary black-box criteria (InterQual, MCG) defeats the rule's transparency goal. Clinical decision logic should be expressed in FHIR PlanDefinitions and CQL, derived from APA, SAMHSA, ASAM, and ASCO society guidelines. Transparency in data exchange without transparency in clinical logic is incomplete reform.
Comment 3 — Episode Pilot: 80.7% of appealed PA denials in MA were overturned in 2024 — the original decision was wrong in the majority of cases (KFF, 2026). I request CMS consider a CMMI demonstration of Episode-Based Behavioral Health Authorization: one PA decision at intake covering the full 90-day episode including evaluation, medication, inpatient stabilization if indicated, PHP, IOP, and follow-up. FHIR-native, society-guideline-anchored, licensed-clinician-governed, compliant with MD HB 1563 and WA SB 5395. Full technical model attached.
Comment 4 — National Scale: This model applies identically to wound care (WOCN/AHRQ) and oncology (ASCO Living Guideline 2026). CMS has the opportunity to establish behavioral health as the proof-of-concept for a national episode authorization standard — one episode, one authorization, one decision — across the full spectrum of care.
Please refer to attached documents for the full technical model and APA-formatted policy analysis.
Joanne Bayouk, MBA, MSN, RN, PMHNP | Just Care | justcare.substack.com | @Just_Care_ | Suwanee, Georgia | June 2026
