title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I strongly support CMS efforts to modernize the prior authorization process and reduce unnecessary administrative barriers to care. Specifically from a workforce and employer perspective,I encourage CMS to ensure that the final rule delivers meaningful operational improvement rather than simply digitizing existing inefficiencies.

Nearly 50 million working Americans are simultaneously serving as family caregivers while managing full-time employment responsibilities.
Delays, denials, repetitive documentation requests, and unclear authorization processes often require caregivers to spend hours coordinating care, contacting insurers, navigating appeals, and managing treatment disruptions.

These burdens affect not only patients and families, but also workforce productivity, employee wellbeing, absenteeism, retention, and healthcare-related financial stress.

For this reason, I strongly encourage CMS to preserve meaningful response timelines and avoid weakening key implementation requirements during the final rulemaking process. Timely decision-making is essential to reducing disruption for working caregivers and maintaining continuity of care.

I also encourage CMS to maintain strong transparency requirements regarding denial rates, approval timelines, and appeal outcomes. Without measurable accountability, interoperability improvements may improve administrative systems without materially improving patient or caregiver experience.

In addition, CMS should discourage repetitive prior authorization requirements for chronic, stable, or previously approved therapies. Repeated reauthorization requirements frequently consume substantial time for caregivers, providers, and patients without improving care quality.

As automated and AI-assisted authorization systems become more common, CMS should also ensure that technology is used to streamline care access rather than accelerate denials or reduce individualized clinical review.

This proposal presents an important opportunity to improve not only healthcare administration, but also workforce stability and caregiver support across the United States.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
As a three-time cancer survivor living with Lynch Syndrome (MSH2 mutation), I understand firsthand the importance of timely access to laboratory testing. Throughout my cancer journey, laboratory, pathology, biomarker, and genetic testing have guided critical healthcare decisions that impacted my treatment, surveillance, and long-term health outcomes.

Prior authorization requirements can create unnecessary delays in obtaining medically necessary tests. For patients facing a cancer diagnosis or potential disease progression, every day spent waiting for approval can increase anxiety, delay treatment decisions, and postpone access to potentially life-saving interventions.

Biomarker and genomic testing are particularly important in modern cancer care because they help identify targeted therapies, determine eligibility for clinical trials, and support personalized treatment decisions. These tests are often ordered based on established clinical guidelines and evidence-based standards of care. Requiring additional administrative approval for guideline-recommended testing can create barriers that ultimately undermine the promise of precision medicine.

Prior authorization requirements may also disproportionately affect patients in underserved communities, those with limited health literacy, older adults, and individuals who already face challenges navigating a complex healthcare system. Patients should not have to become insurance experts in order to access medically necessary testing recommended by their healthcare providers.

In addition to delays, prior authorization can contribute to duplicated testing, repeated blood draws, additional appointments, and increased administrative burden on clinicians and healthcare staff. These inefficiencies increase costs while adding stress to patients and families already coping with serious illness.

CMS should consider policies that exempt guideline-supported laboratory testing, biomarker testing, and genetic testing from prior authorization requirements when ordered according to nationally recognized clinical guidelines. CMS should also promote greater transparency, faster decision-making timelines, and standardized approval processes to ensure that patients receive timely access to medically necessary care.

As both a Patient and Advocate, I believe healthcare decisions should be driven by clinical evidence and patient need rather than administrative barriers. Timely access to laboratory testing can improve outcomes, reduce disparities, and help ensure that patients receive the right care at the right time.

Had genetic testing been available and utilized more broadly earlier in my family's history, my Lynch Syndrome diagnosis may have been identified sooner, potentially influencing screening decisions and risk management for myself and other family members. Timely access to testing does not just affect one patient—it can affect entire families across generations.

When access to laboratory testing is delayed, diagnosis is delayed. When diagnosis is delayed, treatment is delayed. And when treatment is delayed, patients bear the consequences.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
To Whom It May Concern:
I respectfully submit the following comments regarding CMS-0062-P. I support CMS's efforts to improve prior authorization processes and reduce barriers to healthcare access. As a social work professional serving individuals with disabilities and chronic health conditions, I have observed firsthand the challenges that prior authorization requirements can create for vulnerable populations.
I am specifically commenting on the section addressing prior authorization requirements for Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies (DMEPOS). CMS appropriately recognizes that prior authorization processes may delay access to medically necessary equipment and seeks public feedback on ways to reduce these burdens.
Individuals with disabilities often depend on wheelchairs, prosthetic devices, orthotic equipment, and other assistive technologies to maintain independence, employment, community participation, and health. Delays in obtaining these items can have significant consequences. When prior authorization decisions are delayed, beneficiaries may experience decreased mobility, increased risk of injury, deterioration of health conditions, and reduced quality of life.
I recommend that CMS establish an expedited review process for replacement or modification of previously approved durable medical equipment when medical necessity has already been documented and remains substantially unchanged. Many beneficiaries must repeatedly demonstrate medical necessity for equipment that has long been recognized as essential to daily functioning. This requirement creates administrative burdens for beneficiaries, providers, and payers while offering limited additional value in preventing inappropriate utilization.
Additionally, I recommend that CMS consider multi-year authorization periods for certain categories of durable medical equipment used by individuals with permanent disabilities. Conditions such as spinal cord injuries, limb loss, and congenital disabilities often involve lifelong needs that do not require repeated reassessment. Extended authorization periods could reduce administrative costs while maintaining appropriate program oversight.
I also support CMS's efforts to increase transparency regarding prior authorization decisions and denial explanations. Clear communication regarding the reasons for denial can assist beneficiaries and providers in understanding documentation requirements and pursuing timely appeals when necessary. Transparent decision-making promotes accountability and may reduce unnecessary delays in care.
Finally, I encourage CMS to continue engaging disability advocates, healthcare providers, and social workers during implementation of any final rule. These stakeholders possess valuable practical knowledge regarding the real-world effects of prior authorization requirements and can help identify opportunities for improvement.
Thank you for considering these comments. I appreciate CMS's commitment to improving healthcare access and reducing unnecessary administrative burdens for beneficiaries. I respectfully request that CMS incorporate additional protections for individuals requiring durable medical equipment and other long-term supports as it develops the final rule.
Sincerely,
Heidi Wachtel
MSW Student

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Hello,

I am submitting this comment as an undergraduate student pursuing dual degrees in Public Health and Mathematical Data Science at San Diego State University, where I am also involved in public health research focused on infectious disease modeling, community health impact assessment, and health equity in underserved border communities.

I strongly support the proposed rule's expansion of interoperability standards and electronic prior authorization (ePA) requirements to Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, and CHIP agencies. This rule addresses a critical bottleneck in the healthcare system, one that disproportionately harms the most vulnerable patients.

Prior authorization delays are not "administrative inconveniences". Research has consistently shown that PA burdens fall hardest on Medicaid beneficiaries, who are more likely to be patients of color, low-income, and reliant on community health centers with limited administrative capacity to manage PA workflows. In border communities like those along the San Diego–Tijuana corridor, where I have conducted community health research, these barriers compound existing access inequities. A patient waiting days or weeks for PA approval on a necessary medication may forgo care entirely with downstream consequences for chronic disease management, emergency utilization, and population health outcomes.

The proposed FHIR-based standards for drug PA are a meaningful step toward reducing this burden. Standardized electronic PA workflows would reduce the time providers spend on administrative tasks, accelerate decisions for patients, and generate structured data that public health researchers and policymakers can use to monitor disparities in PA approval rates across demographic groups and plan types.

However, I urge CMS to go further in two areas:

First, the proposed rule should require plans to publicly report PA approval and denial rates, stratified by race, ethnicity, language, and condition type. Without this data transparency, it is impossible to identify and correct discriminatory patterns in PA decision-making. The rule's interoperability infrastructure makes this reporting technically feasible — CMS should require it.

Second, I urge CMS to set meaningful timelines for drug PA decisions that reflect clinical urgency. The proposed rule is an opportunity to establish enforceable standards that protect patients when delays can cause measurable harm.

I commend CMS for advancing this rulemaking and urge the agency to finalize it with strong equity provisions. Health data infrastructure is only as valuable as the health outcomes it produces, and this rule has the potential to meaningfully reduce disparities if implemented with that goal in mind.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Dear CMS,

I am a technology leader and IEEE Senior Member with experience supporting AI adoption across 180 or more organizations in healthcare, enterprise, and public sector environments. My peer reviewed research on secure AI architectures for healthcare critical infrastructure was published at IEEE SoutheastCon 2026, and I have written for Healthcare IT Today on post deployment AI governance. I am submitting this comment based on practical experience with AI driven automation in regulated healthcare environments. My comments focus on sections II.B (Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs) and II.C (Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations).

1. Prior authorization decisions that involve AI need transparency at the decision layer

Prior authorization for drugs is increasingly automated on the payer side. AI is used to triage, recommend, or deny requests before a human ever looks at the file. When AI contributes to a denial or an adverse determination, the specific reason for denial requirements in this rule should extend to the AI layer itself. That means disclosing the model version in use at the time of the decision, the inputs it considered, and whether a human actually reviewed the determination before it was sent out.

The proposed public reporting of denial and appeal metrics is a strong step. Without transparency at the decision layer, though, those metrics will describe the outcome but not how the outcome was produced. Patients, prescribers, and pharmacists receive the answer without the decision process behind it, which limits what any of them can do with the information.

2. FHIR based Prior Authorization API requirements should be paired with AI metadata

The FHIR first direction of this rule, including the proposed adoption of the CRD, DTR, and PAS implementation guides for the Prior Authorization API, is strong. As payers and providers exchange data to support electronic prior authorization for drugs covered under a medical benefit, the data envelope should carry enough metadata to identify when AI was used in a decision path. Existing FHIR resources can be extended to carry this metadata without a redesign of the implementation guides CMS is proposing to require.

This is consistent with where HTI-5 was heading on automated actor recognition and with broader federal AI governance work under the NIST AI RMF. Carrying AI metadata in the same transactions that already carry prior authorization decisions avoids standing up a parallel disclosure channel later.

3. Vendor accountability applies to AI enabled prior authorization

Many impacted payers deploy AI for prior authorization through third party vendors, including pharmacy benefit managers and utilization management vendors. The contracts with those vendors were usually written for traditional rules engines, not adaptive AI. Model updates, training data provenance, and ongoing performance monitoring typically are not covered. As CMS establishes the October 1, 2027 compliance dates, the electronic prior authorization requirements, and the decision timeframes in this rule, it is worth addressing vendor accountability for the AI components of the decision pipeline. Otherwise the impacted payer carries the regulatory burden for behavior it does not fully control, and the provider has no clear entity to engage with when something goes wrong.

4. Continuous monitoring of denial and appeal patterns

The proposed public reporting requirements for prior authorization for drugs would be stronger with a continuous monitoring expectation built in. Impacted payers could track and report on denial rates, appeal reversal rates, and decision timing by drug category and patient population. That kind of monitoring creates an operational feedback loop that helps surface when AI driven systems are producing unintended patterns, rather than waiting for those patterns to show up in complaints, state enforcement, or litigation. It also aligns with the direction the proposed numeric count metrics are already moving in.

Thank you for the opportunity to contribute.

Sincerely,
Pooja Walia
IEEE Senior Member Author, ICLR/ICML Reviewer
Published research: "Building Secure and Trustworthy AI for Healthcare Critical Infrastructure," IEEE SoutheastCon 2026

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
As a healthcare leader responsible for clinical informatics and operational workflows, I strongly support the intent of this proposed rule to modernize prior authorization through improved interoperability and electronic processes. Prior authorization delays are not simply administrative inefficiencies—they directly impact patient care. When approvals are delayed, patients experience postponed treatments, interruptions in medication access, and, in some cases, worsening clinical outcomes. For this reason, the proposed decision timeframes are not just operational benchmarks; they are critical patient safety safeguards. However, the effectiveness of this rule will depend on meaningful enforcement. If payers are not held accountable to consistently meet these timelines, the burden of delay will continue to fall on patients despite the transition to electronic systems.
Additionally, it is essential that payers bear the primary responsibility for the costs and operational lift associated with integration and implementation. Prior authorization requirements originate from payer policies, and the administrative complexity that this rule seeks to address has largely been driven by payer processes. While providers will need to interact with enhanced digital workflows, shifting the cost burden onto health systems would further strain organizations already managing significant clinical and financial pressures. True reform requires clear accountability—both in terms of adherence to required timelines and investment in the infrastructure needed to support interoperability. Without enforceable standards and appropriate allocation of responsibility, there is a risk that these changes will not achieve their intended impact. Ensuring payer accountability will be key to delivering meaningful improvements in efficiency, transparency, and, most importantly, patient care.

To Whom It May Concern:

My name is Ashleigh Parker and I am writing as a cancer patient in remission to urgently request that CMS protect patients from critical care delays and denials caused by rigid prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing.
As a cancer patient since 2019, I understand the speed at which care should be provided to cancer patients. The quicker cancer is found and treated, the better the outcome is for the patient. Biomarker testing improves these outcomes. I am a living example of that.

We commend CMS for its ongoing efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes. We also deeply appreciate the opportunity to provide specific feedback via the Request for Information regarding the impact of prior authorization on timely patient access to medically necessary laboratory testing, as referenced in Section III.E of CMS-0062-P.
I urge CMS to protect oncology patients from delays and denials caused by prior authorization requirements for medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing.

In cancer care, timing is critical. Biomarker and specialty lab results often guide treatment selection, treatment changes, disease monitoring, and clinical trial eligibility. When prior authorization rules require approval before or on the exact specimen collection date, valid specimens may be delayed, rejected, or discarded—even when the patient, physician, and laboratory acted in good faith. This can force repeat blood draws and delay urgent cancer care.

CMS should require health plans to:

1. Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected.
2. Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.
3. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available.
4. Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.
5. Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative.
Cancer patients need timely access to laboratory testing so they and their care teams can make informed, potentially life-saving treatment decisions without unnecessary administrative barriers.

Sincerely,

Ashleigh Parker
Stage 4 Colorectal Cancer Survivor
Olive Branch,MS

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
CMS should advance interoperable electronic exchange of clinical information as part of prior authorization workflows to reduce administrative burden, improve interoperability, and accelerate patient access to therapy. Two complementary approaches could support CMS goals for more efficient and near real-time prior authorization adjudication across pharmacy and medical benefit workflows:
1.Prospective clinical data exchange at the time of prior authorization submission:
As part of the initial prior authorization request from the prescriber, CMS should require the transmission of relevant patient clinical data through interoperable standards, including NCPDP SCRIPT ePA for pharmacy benefit drugs and HL7 FHIR-based prior authorization workflows for medical services and drugs covered under the medical benefit. For pharmacy workflows, Real-Time Benefit Tool (RTBT) capabilities leveraging the NCPDP RTPB standard are necessary to identify the applicable pharmacy benefit, determine whether prior authorization is required, and support routing through the appropriate electronic prior authorization workflow. For medical services and medical-benefit drugs, HL7 FHIR-based workflows can support identification of coverage requirements and facilitate exchange of the clinical information necessary to support prior authorization review. Enabling prospective exchange of structured clinical data at the point of submission would support faster and more accurate prior authorization determinations, reduce manual documentation requests, minimize administrative burden on providers and payers, and promote faster access to therapy and improved patient outcomes.
2.TEFCA-enabled clinical data exchange for prior authorization workflows:
To support both prospective and retrospective prior authorization workflows, CMS and ONC should clarify that prior authorization constitutes an appropriate TEFCA Purpose of Use that permits and requires the exchange of patient clinical data necessary to support prior authorization review and adjudication. Without clear TEFCA policy alignment requiring exchange of clinical information for prior authorization workflows, EHR systems and healthcare organizations may continue to restrict or block sharing of the patient clinical data necessary to support interoperable prior authorization processes. Clarifying TEFCA requirements for prior authorization-related data exchange would enable more consistent sharing of clinical information across pharmacy and medical workflows, reduce provider and payer burden, and advance CMS goals for streamlined and near real-time prior authorization adjudication.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
May 22, 2026

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
Re: CMS-0062-P — Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs
Docket No. CMS-2026-1255

Dear Office of CMS,

I am a retail pharmacist, and I am submitting this comment in support of the proposed rule CMS-0062-P. I work directly with patients, doctors, and insurance companies every day, and I want to share what I see on the ground when it comes to prior authorization for prescription drugs.

The current prior authorization process is slow and burdensome for everyone involved. When a doctor sends a prescription and the drug requires prior authorization, the pharmacy has to call the doctor's office to notify them and then keep calling back to find out whether they have submitted the authorization and whether it has been approved. The pharmacy does not always have visibility into what stage the process is at or whether the doctor has even contacted the insurance company. This follow-up takes up a significant amount of pharmacy staff time that should be spent on patient care. At the same time, CMS estimates that prior authorization costs providers around $34,000 and 700 hours per year in administrative work. While all of this is happening, the patient is sitting and waiting for their medicine with no idea what is going on or how long it will take.

I strongly support moving prior authorization for drugs to a fully electronic process. However, I would like to suggest three specific improvements to make this proposal more effective.

First, patients need to be included in the notification process. Right now, when a prior authorization request is sent to a doctor through systems like CoverMyMeds, the patient receives no notification at all. The proposal should require that when a prior authorization is initiated, the patient automatically receives a notification so they know what is happening and can follow up if needed. Transparency for the patient is just as important as speed.

Second, providers should be given real-time access to each patient's drug formulary before writing a prescription. If a doctor could check what the patient's insurance covers and initiate prior authorization before sending the prescription to the pharmacy, the entire back-and-forth process between the pharmacy and the doctor's office could be avoided. This would save time for both the pharmacy and the provider, and most importantly, it would reduce the wait time for the patient.

Third, I have a concern about the API reporting requirement and the civil monetary penalties attached to it. While I understand the need for accountability, adding penalty-backed reporting requirements creates a new administrative burden for providers. When providers are focused on managing compliance and avoiding penalties, their attention shifts away from patient care, which is the opposite of what this proposal is trying to achieve. I would ask CMS to consider whether there is a simpler way to monitor compliance that does not add to the administrative load that providers are already carrying.

Overall, I believe this proposal is a step in the right direction. The prior authorization process for drugs needs to be modernized, and I am glad CMS is addressing it. I hope these suggestions are helpful, and I appreciate the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am nurse practitioner in Florida. Prior authorization (PA) and step therapy requirements create significant barriers to timely patient care. While utilization management can play a role in promoting evidence-based care, the current processes frequently result in treatment delays, interruptions in therapy, increased administrative burden, and patient frustration. Prior authorization requirements often delay medically necessary treatment while patients wait for payer review and approval. Step therapy policies can require patients to fail therapies that may be less effective or inappropriate for their individual clinical circumstances before accessing the treatment recommended by their clinician.
These challenges are particularly burdensome for physician-administered therapies, where delays can postpone treatment initiation and worsen patient outcomes. In addition, health plans may implement coverage policy changes with limited advance notice, creating confusion for patients and providers and disrupting continuity of care.
Specific Patient Example
One of my patients required a physician-administered therapy that I determined was medically appropriate based on clinical guidelines and the patient's treatment history. However, the patient's health plan required prior authorization and additional documentation. The approval process took several weeks, during which the patient's symptoms worsened and additional office visits were required. Significant staff time was also spent responding to payer requests and appeals. Ultimately, the therapy was approved, but the delay created unnecessary burden for both the patient and the care team.
Provisions of the Proposed Rule I Support
I strongly support several aspects of CMS's proposed rule.
Faster prior authorization decisions: More timely determinations would help reduce treatment delays and improve patient access to medically necessary care. CMS has proposed measures intended to accelerate payer decision-making and improve the prior authorization process.
Expanded electronic prior authorization (e-PA): Requiring standardized electronic prior authorization processes and APIs has the potential to reduce administrative burden, improve workflow efficiency, and facilitate real-time information exchange between providers and health plans.
Greater health plan transparency: Public reporting of prior authorization metrics and clearer communication regarding denials will help providers and patients better understand coverage requirements and hold plans accountable for timely and appropriate decision-making.
Recommendations for CMS to Strengthen the Rule
I encourage CMS to further strengthen the rule by:
Requiring advance notice of coverage policy and formulary changes that affect physician-administered therapies.
Limiting step therapy requirements when evidence supports the prescribed therapy or when patients have already demonstrated failure, intolerance, or contraindications to alternative treatments.
Ensuring that prior authorization and step therapy decisions are based on current clinical evidence and specialty-specific guidelines.
Expanding protections that preserve continuity of care when patients change health plans.
Requiring greater transparency around approval, denial, and overturn rates for both prior authorization and step therapy requests.
Establishing stronger oversight and accountability mechanisms when plans fail to meet required response timeframes.
Closing
As a nurse practitioner, I support CMS's efforts to modernize prior authorization through faster decisions, expanded electronic prior authorization capabilities, and increased transparency. These reforms can help reduce administrative burden and improve patient access to timely, evidence-based care. However, additional protections are needed to ensure that prior authorization and step therapy policies do not interfere with clinically appropriate treatment decisions made by healthcare providers in partnership with their patients. Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Re: CMS-0062-P, 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs (91 FR 19890)

EVRESA LLC (Enterprise Verification - Regulated E-Settlement Architecture) submits the attached public comment package on CMS-0062-P, RIN 0938-AV44: a foundational comment, three RFI responses, and an Operational Impact Statement on independent community pharmacy. EVRESA is an AI-governance infrastructure developer building CATN, the Care Access Trust Network by EVRESA, a governance and decision-provenance layer for prior authorization. EVRESA submits this comment as a developer of governance infrastructure, not as a payer or provider; our perspective is architectural.

EVRESA strongly supports extending electronic prior authorization to drugs, aligning decision timeframes, and requiring a specific reason for each denial. EVRESA writes to identify one implementation gap that will determine whether these gains are durable: the proposed rule standardizes the transaction of a prior authorization decision, but not the governance proof layer needed to establish accountability for that decision where automated or AI-enabled tools are used.

To meet 72-hour and 24-hour timeframes, impacted payers and technology partners may increasingly place automated, rules-based, or AI-enabled systems in the decision loop. A specific denial reason is necessary, but it is not sufficient by itself. A denial reason does not establish who or what rendered the decision, whether AI contributed, what evidence was reviewed, under whose authority the decision was made, or whether a qualified human remained accountable at the decision point. Without governance-layer controls, a denial reason can become a machine-generated field attached to an unaccountable automated decision.

EVRESA recommends that CMS recognize, in the final rule preamble or subsequent implementation guidance, privacy-preserving governance-layer controls above the transaction layer standardized by CMS-0062-P. These controls should include decision provenance, human-authority attestation, tamper-evident audit records, evidence-chain integrity, and a verifiable chain of custody for decision evidence.

First, CMS should encourage decision provenance records for drug prior authorization determinations where automated or AI-enabled tools are used, including a structured, machine-verifiable record of which system rendered or supported the decision, whether AI contributed, what evidence was reviewed, and which human authority was accountable for the outcome.

Second, CMS should encourage denial reasons to be bound to provenance records where feasible, so appeals, audits, and oversight can verify that a denial was not an unreviewed automated action.

Third, in response to RFI III.B on Increasing Health Care Resiliency, CMS should treat the integrity and auditability of the prior authorization decision record as a resiliency control. Resiliency is not only uptime; it is the ability to prove, after the fact, that decisions affecting patient access were made under valid authority through a verifiable chain of custody for decision evidence.

Fourth, CMS should encourage testable governance outcomes. Provenance, human-authority, evidence-chain, and tamper-evident audit controls should be verifiable through implementation testing, not self-attestation alone.

These recommendations do not require CMS to mandate EVRESA, CATN, or any specific vendor, platform, ledger, or architecture. They define a vendor-neutral outcome: where automated or AI-enabled tools are used, every prior authorization decision should be attributable, authority-bound, evidence-linked, privacy-preserving, and auditable. EVRESA's design pattern operationalizes this principle as Human Authority, Enforced at Machine Speed, and is offered as one reference model among many possible implementations.

As CMS modernizes prior authorization to protect patient access, the same automation that creates speed also creates a new governance risk: speed without accountability. Governance-layer controls allow CMS and the healthcare ecosystem to capture the benefits of automation while preserving the human authority, evidence integrity, privacy, and auditability that make prior authorization decisions trustworthy.

Respectfully submitted,

John Gray Rodriguez
Founder & Chief Executive Officer
EVRESA LLC
Care Access Trust Network (CATN) by EVRESA

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am writing to submit comments on the proposed rule CMS-0062-P. I am a rheumatologist in Seattle, Washington, and I conduct research on prior authorization barriers in rheumatology, including published studies on tocilizumab access delays in giant cell arteritis and carrier-level variation in PA approval rates for biologic medications. I submit these comments as an individual physician and researcher.
I strongly support the goals of this proposed rule.
I. Clinical Urgency: Drug PA in Rheumatology Cannot Wait 7 Days
PA delays for biologic medications cause measurable patient harm. Visual loss in Giant Cell Arteritis can occur within hours. A 7-calendar-day standard decision window for non-urgent drug PA may be insufficient for this and similar conditions requiring urgent biologics. (Bays et al., J Rheumatol 2025, PMID 40089304.)
Recommendation:
• Create an explicit expedited drug PA pathway for conditions with acute risk of organ damage or death, with a 24-48 hour decision standard.
• Define expedited eligibility criteria that include vision-threatening disease, acute inflammatory flares with functional impairment, and other conditions where delay risks irreversible harm.

II. Electronic Transmission Is Not Enough — Denial Content Must Be Meaningful
Electronic submission of inadequate denial rationales does not advance transparency. In research analyzing Washington State's mandatory PA transparency dataset — the only publicly available drug-level PA dataset in the United States — I found approval rates for the same biologic drug ranging from 2.3% to 100% across carriers, a 44-fold variation that cannot be explained by clinical appropriateness alone. Opaque, inconsistent decision-making is not cured by digitizing it.
Recommendation: Require that drug PA denial notices include:
• The specific formulary criterion or clinical policy provision that was not met, cited by name and version.
• Whether the denial is based on step therapy, and which specific prior drug trials are required.
• Whether an AI or algorithmic tool was used in the decision, and if so, which system.
• The name and specialty of the reviewing clinician for peer-to-peer denials.

Generic 'not medically necessary' denials communicated electronically are no improvement over paper denials. The rule should specify minimum content standards for denial explanations.
III. Step Therapy for Biologics Requires Specific Standards
Step therapy — requiring patients to fail on a lower-cost drug before a prescribed biologic is authorized — is one of the most disruptive PA practices in rheumatology. It delays guideline-concordant care and in some cases results in preventable joint damage or organ injury during the mandated 'fail first' period.
Recommendation:
• Require payers to publish step therapy protocols for each drug at each formulary tier in a standardized, machine-readable format.
• Establish gold card exemptions for patients with documented completion of required step therapy in prior claims data, eliminating redundant re-authorization for the same drug class.
• Prohibit prospective re-trials of drugs a patient has already documented failure on.

IV. Drug-Level PA Data Should Be Publicly Reported
Washington State's mandatory PA transparency law is the only mechanism in the United States producing drug-specific, carrier-level PA approval and denial data. The variation it reveals — which is not visible in aggregate statistics — is essential for accountability and health services research. CMS is positioned to create a centralized, publicly accessible drug PA data repository that does not currently exist at the federal level.
Recommendation: Require public reporting of drug PA metrics at the drug-specific and carrier-specific level, and establish a centralized CMS repository for this data — modeled on the transparency provisions of state laws like Washington's ESSB 6404.

CMS-0062-P is an important step toward holding payers accountable for drug PA practices that cause measurable patient harm. Strengthening the rule with expedited pathways for urgent biologics, meaningful denial content standards, step therapy transparency, an accelerated Medicare Advantage timeline, and drug-level public reporting would substantially improve outcomes for patients with autoimmune and rheumatic diseases.
I am grateful for the opportunity to comment and am available to provide additional information.
Respectfully submitted,
Dr. Bays

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am a registered nurse with 5.5 years of clinical experience across multiple disciplines and an independent clinical AI governance consultant. I am submitting this comment in connection with primary-source research I have conducted on CMS-0057-F prior authorization disclosures.

Under CMS-0057-F, impacted payers were required to publicly report prior authorization denial rates for non-drug items and services beginning March 31, 2026. In reviewing these disclosures directly from payer websites, I identified a material disclosure quality problem: UnitedHealthcare's HTML disclosure pages present "PA rate" — the percentage of claims requiring prior authorization — in the same visual format as the CMS-required denial rate, without clear labeling distinguishing these metrics. These are mathematically different measures with different denominators. This distinction is particularly important when the disclosures are used for cross-payer comparison, benchmarking, or future analytic applications. A reader relying solely on the HTML disclosure page may not readily identify the CMS-required denial rate without consulting additional disclosure materials. This finding is documented as Infrastructure Finding IF-002 in a publicly available primary-source dataset I have published at https://github.com/sole-healthtech/cms-0057f-prior-auth.

CMS-0062-P proposes to extend the prior authorization transparency framework to drugs. I strongly support this expansion. However, I urge CMS to address disclosure quality standards alongside disclosure requirements. If impacted payers can satisfy the transparency requirement by publishing metrics that conflate different measures — as documented in the non-drug context — extending the framework to drugs will replicate the same structural problem at greater scale. I recommend that CMS specify in the final rule that publicly reported prior authorization metrics must include clear labeling distinguishing PA rate from denial rate, and that raw counts sufficient to verify reported rates must be included alongside percentage figures.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am a Georgia patient and a survivor of severe traumatic brain injury and major orthopedic trauma. During rehabilitation, I saw how dependent recovery is on approvals, coverage, timing, and continuity of care. In rehabilitation and follow-up care, delay is not administrative. Delay is clinical. Skills like walking, transferring safely, eating independently, and rebuilding balance require repeated care at the right time. When coverage or authorization delays interrupt that process, patients can lose function they may never regain.

I support CMS’s efforts to make prior authorization more timely, transparent, and interoperable. However, electronic prior authorization must not simply make denials faster or harder to challenge. A rapid electronic denial still harms patients if they cannot understand the reason, correct the record, appeal quickly, or obtain care while it can still preserve function.

Clear, specific, clinically meaningful denial explanations, not generic “documentation insufficient” language.

Accessible prior authorization records, including request date, documents submitted, status changes, decision date, denial reason, appeal pathway, and final outcome.

Metrics that measure real patient impact, including time to care, appeal time, repeat-request burden, abandoned care, and delays affecting function.

Safeguards for automated or electronic systems, so these tools do not create opaque denials, hidden delays, or records patients cannot correct.

Special attention to rehabilitation, imaging, therapy, lab testing, and DMEPOS, where timing and continuity may determine whether a patient regains or preserves basic function.

For many patients, a delayed approval or broken care pathway does not simply postpone treatment. It can cause functional loss and higher downstream costs.

The central question is not only whether prior authorization becomes electronic. The central question is whether care reaches the patient in time.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Date: June 10, 2026
To: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services
Attention: Docket ID: CMS-2026-1255
Reference: RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory Testing (Section III.E of CMS-0062-P)
Submission Portal: Regulations.gov (https://www.regulations.gov/)
Re: Comment on RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory Testing

To Whom It May Concern:
My name is Marva Steed and I am writing as a patient to urgently request that CMS protect patients from critical care delays and denials caused by rigid prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing, specifically biomarker testing in addition to ongoing Signatera testing to confirm I have no further cancer cells in my blood.
I was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2022 and denied a pet scan and several pathology testing protocols requested by my oncologist.
We commend CMS for its ongoing efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes. We also deeply appreciate the opportunity to provide specific feedback via the Request for Information regarding the impact of prior authorization on timely patient access to medically necessary laboratory testing, as referenced in Section III.E of CMS-0062-P.
I urge CMS to protect oncology patients from delays and denials caused by prior authorization requirements for medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing.
In cancer care, timing is critical. Biomarker and specialty lab results often guide treatment selection, treatment changes, disease monitoring, and clinical trial eligibility. When prior authorization rules require approval before or on the exact specimen collection date, valid specimens may be delayed, rejected, or discarded—even when the patient, physician, and laboratory acted in good faith. This can force repeat blood draws and delay urgent cancer care.
CMS should require health plans to:
1. Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected.
2. Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.
3. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available.
4. Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.
5. Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative.
Cancer patients need timely access to laboratory testing so they and their care teams can make informed, potentially life-saving treatment decisions without unnecessary administrative barriers.
Sincerely,
Marva S

comment: I am responding to the request for comments on the question, "Would requiring impacted payers to make information available using both standards add value, or create additional burden, specifically related to electronic prior authorization of drugs?" title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Lab prior authorization requirement creates severe barriers by causing dangerous delays in treatment, abandonment of care, and staggering administrative burdens that divert medical staff away from direct patient care.
The barriers created by this process include:
1. Treatment and Diagnostic Delays
•Time-to-Diagnosis: Waiting days or weeks for insurance approval delays vital test results (such as genetic and infectious disease screening), directly postponing life-saving treatments.
•Therapy Abandonment: The friction and extensive wait times often lead to patients abandoning recommended testing and care altogether.
2. Administrative Burden
•Staff Burnout: Navigating complex payer protocols, repeated phone calls, and manual paperwork diverts hours of physician and staff time away from patient-facing activities.
•Coding and Clerical Errors: Simple administrative errors—such as incorrect billing codes or slight typos in a submission—frequently result in automatic test denials.
3. Compromised Clinical Care
•Forced Alternative Treatments: Payers may require providers to use less-expensive, non-indicated testing methods before covering the initially prescribed test.
•Adverse Health Events: When physicians alter clinical decisions to avoid prior authorization friction, or when crucial labs are denied, patients face serious downstream health complications and increased hospitalizations.
4. Patient Financial Risk
•Surprise Out-of-Pocket Costs: A denied prior authorization often means the patient is unexpectedly billed the full cost of the laboratory service if the test is still processed without the insurer's green light.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am submitting this comment as a private citizen. I am a software architect who served as a voting member of the HL7 Standards Committee. I contributed to the v2.3 ADT, SIU, and ORM messages, and later designed and operated a high-throughput HL7 integration engine that carried more than 800 live production interfaces across EHRs, laboratories, and e-prescription partners.

My comments are limited to a single interoperability mechanic in the proposed rule.

I support the goal of requiring electronic prior authorization for drugs. The recommendations below are intended to help the dual-standard architecture in the rule survive contact with a real network of payers and providers.

Standard selection (medical vs pharmacy benefit) is an unsolved routing problem; make path determination a required capability, not an optional convention.

The proposed rule establishes two mutually exclusive standard sets for drug prior authorization: the FHIR-based Prior Authorization API (Da Vinci) for drugs covered under a medical benefit, and the NCPDP standards for drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit. The PAS IG itself states it "SHOULD NOT be used for any medication that is covered under a pharmacy benefit where prior authorization is provided by another electronic exchange process (for example, NCPDP SCRIPT)."

The rule also acknowledges (correctly) that "there is currently no statutory or regulatory definition that distinguishes between drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit and drugs covered under a medical benefit," that the same drug can fall into different categories for different payers based on their terms of coverage, and that this classification can change over time. The rule's proposed remedy is that impacted payers "could indicate which method a provider should use to submit a particular prior authorization."

"Could" is the problem, from an integration standpoint. The rule routes by default the standard-selection decision to the requesting system (provider or EHR), while leaving the authoritative signal that would make that decision correct optional. On a network where each provider transacts with many payers, an optional/undefined signal produces predictable failure: requests submitted on the wrong standard, rejected or silently dropped, fallback to fax/phone, which is the burden this rule exists to remove. Misrouting a request across two incompatible stacks is worse for patients and providers than a single slower path, because the requester often can't detect if the failure was a routing error.

This is a classic message-routing problem, and the established solution is to centralize the routing decision in one authoritative lookup rather than re-deriving it at every endpoint.

I recommend that CMS require that same first-stage CRD response to also return, in machine-readable form, *which* standard and endpoint the requester must use for that drug, for that patient, under that payer's coverage.

In closing, I support electronic prior authorization for drugs and the broader interoperability direction of this rule. The recommendation above is narrow: make the choice between the two mandated standards an authoritative, machine-readable answer the payer returns. Thank you for considering this comment.

Respectfully submitted,

Scott Underwood
Software architect; former voting member, HL7 Standards Committee (HL7 v2.3 ADT, SIU, ORM)

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am writing as both a provider who has been in practice for 26 years and as a daughter of a patient who's care was delayed as a result of waiting on prior authorization through Medicare. I strongly support CMS-0062-P and urge CMS to finalize and strengthen it. Doctors and other treating clinicians—not insurance companies—should decide what care patients need based on clinical evidence, medical necessity, and the patient's individual circumstances.

Prior authorization too often functions as denial by delay. Patients cannot afford to wait while paperwork, portals, faxes, or payer-specific rules stand between them and medically necessary treatment. Delays can interrupt medication access, postpone diagnoses, increase anxiety, and worsen outcomes, especially for patients with cancer, chronic illness, pregnancy-related needs, or complex conditions that require timely medication access or diagnostic testing.

The burden is well documented. MACPAC reports that physician practices complete an average of 43 prior authorization requests per physician each week, requiring about 12 hours of physician and staff time. That is time diverted away from direct patient care. Research in cancer care has also documented prior authorization-related delays of two weeks or longer and cases where patients did not receive care recommended by their treatment team. This is not an inconvenience; it is a patient access problem.

I support CMS's proposal to extend electronic prior authorization and interoperability standards to drugs. Standardized electronic workflows, real-time exchange of coverage and documentation requirements, and shorter decision timeframes can reduce administrative burden and help patients receive needed care faster. However, electronic submission alone will not be enough if payers can still use vague criteria, repeated requests for information, unclear denials, or slow appeals to delay care.
I urge CMS to strengthen the final rule by:

1. Requiring 24-hour prior authorization decisions for all drugs and for time-sensitive care, including oncology care and diagnostic/laboratory testing. At a minimum, expedited requests should be decided within 24 hours, and standard requests should not exceed 72 hours. If a payer fails to meet the required timeframe, the request should be deemed approved or covered until review is completed.

2. Clearly defining a complete prior authorization submission. Once a provider or laboratory submits the required information through the standardized process, the review clock should begin. Payers should not be allowed to restart the clock with duplicative, non-clinical, or previously undisclosed documentation demands.

3. Mandating clear, specific, actionable denial explanations for every denial. Denials should identify the exact policy or clinical criterion relied upon, explain why the documentation did not meet that requirement, state what information is missing if applicable, and provide plain-language instructions for reconsideration or appeal.

4. Ensuring a robust and timely appeals process. Appeals should be simple to file electronically, decided quickly enough to prevent harm, and reviewed by appropriately qualified clinicians with relevant expertise. The treating clinician's judgment should be given substantial weight.

5. Strengthening protections for laboratory testing. Payers should not be permitted to deny a medically necessary test solely because authorization was pending on the date a blood draw or specimen collection occurred. Patients should not be forced into unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is already available, nor should patients, clinicians, or laboratories face financial penalties caused by payer paperwork delays.

6. Expanding transparency and accountability. Payers should publicly report approval rates, denial rates, turnaround times, appeal rates, appeal outcomes, overturn rates, and common denial reasons in a meaningful, plan-specific and service-specific way.

CMS-0062-P is an important step toward a more transparent, efficient, and patient-centered prior authorization system. I strongly urge CMS to finalize and strengthen this rule so that medical decisions remain centered on patients and their treating clinicians, not administrative barriers or insurance company delay tactics.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am submitting this comment as a private citizen. I'm a software architect who served as a voting member of the HL7 Standards Committee. I contributed to the v2.3 ADT, SIU, and ORM messages, and later designed and operated a high-throughput HL7 integration engine that carried more than 800 live production interfaces across EHRs, laboratories, and e-prescription partners.

My comments are limited to a single interoperability mechanic in the proposed rule.

I support the goal of requiring electronic prior authorization for drugs. The recommendations below are intended to help the dual-standard architecture in the rule survive contact with a real network of payers and providers.

Standard selection (medical vs pharmacy benefit) is an unsolved routing problem; make path determination a required capability, not an optional convention.

The proposed rule establishes two mutually exclusive standard sets for drug prior authorization: the FHIR-based Prior Authorization API (Da Vinci) for drugs covered under a medical benefit, and the NCPDP standards for drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit. The PAS IG itself states it "SHOULD NOT be used for any medication that is covered under a pharmacy benefit where prior authorization is provided by another electronic exchange process (for example, NCPDP SCRIPT)."

The rule also acknowledges (correctly) that "there is currently no statutory or regulatory definition that distinguishes between drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit and drugs covered under a medical benefit," that the same drug can fall into different categories for different payers based on their terms of coverage, and that this classification can change over time. The rule's proposed remedy is that impacted payers "could indicate which method a provider should use to submit a particular prior authorization."

"Could" is the problem, from an integration standpoint. The rule routes by default the standard-selection decision to the requesting system (provider or EHR), while leaving the authoritative signal that would make that decision correct optional. On a network where each provider transacts with many payers, an optional/undefined signal produces predictable failure: requests submitted on the wrong standard, rejected or silently dropped, fallback to fax/phone, which is the burden this rule exists to remove. Misrouting a request across two incompatible stacks is worse for patients and providers than a single slower path, because the requester often can't detect if the failure was a routing error.

This is a classic message-routing problem, and the established solution is to centralize the routing decision in one authoritative lookup rather than re-deriving it at every endpoint.

I recommend that CMS require that same first-stage CRD response to also return, in machine-readable form, *which* standard and endpoint the requester must use for that drug, for that patient, under that payer's coverage.

In closing, I support electronic prior authorization for drugs and the broader interoperability direction of this rule. The recommendation above is narrow: make the choice between the two mandated standards an authoritative, machine-readable answer the payer returns. Thank you for considering this comment.

Respectfully submitted,

Scott Underwood
Software architect; former voting member, HL7 Standards Committee (HL7 v2.3 ADT, SIU, ORM)

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am writing to submit my strong support for this proposed rule, which takes critical steps toward modernizing healthcare data exchange and lowering administrative barriers for both patients and providers.
First, I want to applaud the Trump Administration for its continued leadership on this front. This administration has done more than any past presidency to aggressively advance the interoperability of electronic health records (EHRs). By treating healthcare data silos as a barrier to competitive markets and patient freedom, this administration is fundamentally reshaping how healthcare operates in America. Extending these interoperability standards to prescription drug prior authorizations is a natural and highly necessary continuation of that legacy.
These technical advancements will have a massive, direct benefit on patients and the overall cost of care. For too long, patients have suffered from delayed treatments, duplicate testing, and administrative bottlenecks because different health IT systems refuse to speak to one another. Embracing FHIR standards and streamlining the prior authorization process will allow true care to happen seamlessly. When records flow freely, it reduces administrative overhead, prevents medical errors, eliminates wasteful repeating of tests, and ultimately drives down the cost of care for hard-working Americans.
However, to truly achieve the administration's vision of full interoperability, we must address the remaining roadblocks in the private EHR sector. I strongly encourage President Trump to leverage his relationship with Oracle Chairman Larry Ellison to push Oracle Cerner to do much more to make its EHR platform fully interoperable.
Currently, there is a stark divide in user and patient experience between platforms. Epic has dedicated significant focus to active, patient-driven interoperability through MyChart Central, an innovation that seamlessly links multiple patient accounts and automatically updates and syncs patient demographics and medical history across entirely different healthcare organizations. 
In contrast, Oracle Cerner remains technically lagging; it routinely struggles to seamlessly import records from competing platforms like Epic, leaving providers blind to parts of a patient's medical history. Cerner lacks the dynamic interoperability found in MyChart Central and is technically a weaker EHR platform because of these integration deficiencies. If Oracle is truly committed to the American healthcare system, Mr. Ellison must align Cerner's capabilities with this administration's mandate for open, frictionless data exchange.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important rule and for your ongoing commitment to putting patients first through technological innovation.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Patients Rising is a national patient advocacy organization. For more than ten years we have worked alongside patients and caregivers living with serious and chronic illness, and through our Learning Center we provide navigation support as needed and, above all, help patients learn to advocate for themselves within the coverage system. We write in support of the overall direction of the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P), which begins to treat prior authorization as infrastructure to be fixed rather than a permanent fact of patient life.

The case for reform is in CMS's own data: in 2024, Medicare Advantage insurers made nearly 53 million prior authorization determinations and denied 4.1 million — yet of the small share of denials that were appealed, more than 80 percent were overturned (KFF analysis of CMS data). Most patients never appeal; they simply absorb a "no" that was often wrong. In the American Medical Association's national physician survey, the large majority of physicians reported that prior authorization delays necessary care and drives patients to abandon treatment, and more than one in four reported it has caused a serious adverse event.

Our full comment is attached. In brief, we urge CMS to: (1) require electronic prior authorization across the medical and pharmacy benefit, with status visible to patients; (2) require 24-hour determinations paired with oversight against auto-denials; (3) require plain-language denial justifications to patients and providers for every denial; (4) require public, plan-level reporting, including Part D, broken out by brand/generic and therapeutic area; (5) on step therapy, decline to let Medicare Advantage plans expand it, honor steps already completed across plans, and keep it transparent; and (6) on laboratory testing, end timing-based denials, accept the test requisition form as valid documentation, and examine the role of laboratory benefit managers.

We thank CMS for advancing patient-centered reform and welcome the chance to be a constructive resource.

— Terry Wilcox, Co-Founder & CEO, Patients Rising

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Re: CMS-0062-P – Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Interoperability, Electronic Prior Authorization, and Patient Access Proposed Rule

To the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services:

I am Bo Wang, MD, a practicing medical oncologist, and I appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on CMS-0062-P. I strongly support CMS's efforts to modernize prior authorization processes, improve interoperability, and reduce administrative barriers that delay medically necessary care. I am particularly encouraged by CMS's Request for Information regarding prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing and their impact on patient care.

In oncology, laboratory and pathology testing are not ancillary services—they are essential components of diagnosis, staging, treatment selection, and ongoing disease monitoring. Modern cancer care increasingly relies on molecular diagnostics, biomarker testing, genomic profiling, pathology review, and serial laboratory assessments to guide evidence-based treatment decisions. Delays in obtaining these tests can directly delay diagnosis, postpone treatment initiation, and adversely affect patient outcomes.

Unfortunately, prior authorization requirements frequently create barriers to timely testing. In my clinical practice, I have encountered situations in which medically necessary laboratory or pathology tests are delayed or denied because an authorization was still pending when a specimen was collected. These timing-based denials occur despite the fact that the test was clinically appropriate, ordered by a treating physician, and performed on a valid specimen. Such administrative denials do not improve patient care or reduce inappropriate utilization. Instead, they create unnecessary burdens for patients, providers, and laboratories.

For cancer patients, the consequences can be particularly harmful. When insurers refuse to authorize testing after a specimen has already been collected, patients may be forced to undergo repeat blood draws or additional invasive procedures solely because of administrative delays. This can cause physical discomfort, emotional distress, delays in treatment planning, and increased healthcare costs. In some cases, repeat specimen collection may not be feasible or may require additional procedures that expose patients to avoidable risk.

I therefore urge CMS to adopt patient-centered policies that specifically address prior authorization barriers affecting laboratory and pathology testing. In particular, CMS should:

• Prohibit denials based solely on the timing of specimen collection when a medically necessary test has been ordered and a valid specimen has already been obtained.

• Prevent insurers from requiring repeat blood draws, tissue sampling, or other specimen collection solely because prior authorization was pending at the time the specimen was collected.

• Establish expedited review pathways for oncology-related laboratory, pathology, molecular diagnostic, and biomarker testing where delays may affect treatment decisions or patient outcomes.

• Require payers to provide transparent, clinically meaningful explanations for laboratory testing denials and make those explanations available through electronic prior authorization systems.

• Protect patients, physicians, and laboratories from financial penalties, claim denials, or surprise billing that result from payer administrative delays rather than clinical considerations.

• Require reporting and public transparency regarding laboratory and pathology testing prior authorization denial rates, turnaround times, and overturn rates on appeal.

The broader interoperability and electronic prior authorization provisions proposed by CMS represent important progress. However, the success of these reforms should ultimately be measured by whether patients receive timely access to medically necessary care. Laboratory and pathology testing are foundational to modern cancer treatment, and prior authorization policies should facilitate—not obstruct—the delivery of these critical services.

I commend CMS for recognizing the challenges associated with prior authorization requirements for laboratory testing and encourage the agency to use this rulemaking opportunity to establish stronger protections for patients facing serious illnesses, including cancer.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Sincerely,

Bo Wang, MD
Medical Oncologist

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Date: June 11, 2026

To: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
Re: CMS-0062-P — Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs
Reference: 91 FR 19890 (Apr. 14, 2026); Document No. 2026-07205

Subject: Comment on Prior Authorization Requirements and Access to Medically Necessary Laboratory Testing

My name is Michelle DeAngelo, and I submit this comment as a patient advocate, healthcare professional, and representative of The Cholangiocarcinoma Foundation. I urge CMS to strengthen prior authorization reforms to prevent delays and denials of medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing and to better protect patients with serious, time-sensitive conditions.

As the daughter of a woman who died from cholangiocarcinoma in 2003 and a healthcare professional with 19 years of experience, I have seen the consequences of delayed testing firsthand. When testing is postponed, patients can lose critical time to begin treatment, adjust therapy, or pursue potentially life-saving options.

CMS should clarify that patients with cancer must have timely access to medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing without delays, step therapy requirements, or denials based on outdated eligibility criteria. Coverage and authorization policies should not rely on assumptions related to age or family history that may no longer reflect current evidence or the realities of cancer diagnosis. As rare cancers such as cholangiocarcinoma are increasingly diagnosed in younger adults, prior authorization policies should reflect contemporary clinical practice and support evidence-based care. These considerations are especially important because delays in testing can directly compromise treatment planning and other time-sensitive aspects of cancer care.

In cancer care, biomarker and specialty laboratory testing inform treatment selection, treatment modification, disease monitoring, and clinical trial eligibility. Prior authorization requirements tied to the date of specimen collection can result in valid specimens being delayed, rejected, or discarded, even when the patient, clinician, and laboratory have acted appropriately. These administrative barriers can require repeat blood draws, delay clinical decision-making, and result in missed treatment opportunities. Recent real-world research found that biomarker testing rates among patients with advanced cancer remained only 35% despite guideline recommendations, underscoring ongoing barriers to timely, appropriate care.

Additional patient harms and policy concerns warrant explicit attention. If approval is not granted by the date of specimen collection, laboratories may be forced to discard valid specimens, resulting in unnecessary repeat blood draws and avoidable clinical risk. These policies misalign administrative processes with clinical realities: patients, physicians, and laboratories acting in good faith should not be penalized because of insurer processing delays, and clerical deadlines should not override documented medical necessity. The consequences also extend beyond clinical care, including unexpected out-of-network charges, lost wages, travel expenses, and childcare costs associated with repeat testing. These burdens fall especially hard on rural, low-income, medically underserved, immunocompromised, and severely ill patients. CMS should require review standards that support expedited decision-making and reflect real-world laboratory workflows rather than rigid administrative timelines.

To address these harms, CMS should require health plans to adopt safeguards that protect patients and preserve timely access to appropriate cancer care:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the impact of prior authorization requirements on timely access to medically necessary laboratory testing under Section III.E of CMS-0062-P.

I respectfully urge CMS to adopt prior authorization policies that prevent avoidable testing delays and protect patients with serious, time-sensitive conditions.

Sincerely,
Michelle DeAngelo
Patient Advocate and Healthcare Professional
The Cholangiocarcinoma Foundation

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
The Long-Term Post-Acute Care (LTPAC) Health IT Collaborative submits these comments on the proposed rule on Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs (CMS-0062-P), published in the Federal Register on April 14, 2026 (Vol. 91, No. 71). The Collaborative's members include provider and professional associations and national experts representing nursing facilities, skilled nursing facilities, assisted living, home health, hospice, continuing care retirement communities, rehabilitation services, pharmacy, nursing, and healthcare information systems.

Established in 2005 to advance health IT issues through coordination among LTPAC provider organizations, policymakers, vendors, payers, and other stakeholders, the Collaborative has consistently advocated for policies that reflect the unique care and technology environments of LTPAC providers and the complex, high-need patients they serve. For more than two decades, the Collaborative has engaged with every major federal health IT and interoperability rulemaking, including the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057), the ONC HTI-2 rulemaking, and the HITAC Affordability Hearing on administrative workflows held May 7, 2026, on behalf of the care settings and populations most often underrepresented in federal health IT policy.

The Collaborative strongly supports the goals of CMS-0062-P: standardizing electronic prior authorization (ePA) for drugs, reducing administrative burden on providers, shortening prior authorization decision timeframes, and increasing payer transparency. We offer the following comments to ensure the final rule achieves these goals equitably across the full care continuum.

In summary, affordability, modernization, and consumer choice cannot be achieved for older Americans without intentionally designing solutions for LTPAC. We face 63+ payers in a single facility, a 15-year technology investment gap from HITECH exclusion, mandatory care obligations that make prior authorization delays a patient safety issue, and only 17% of hospitals sending interoperable data to us. We support today's innovation and modernization agenda. We simply ask that success be measured by whether it reaches the skilled nursing facility, home health agency, hospice, and other post-acute care settings, not just the hospital and physician practice.

Premier Inc. appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Medicare Program; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges), CMS-0062-P. Premier appreciates the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)’ ongoing commitment to improving access to care and enabling better data exchange among providers, patients and payers.

In our detailed comments below, Premier specifically recommends that CMS:

•Finalize its proposed policy to require that impacted payers support electronic prior authorization (ePA) for all drugs that require prior authorization which would align with non-drug ePA policies.
•Finalize the proposed timeline for drug prior authorization (requiring payers to respond within 72-hours for standard requests, and 24 hours for urgent requests) for Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers and shorten the existing timelines for non-drug prior authorization to advance greater alignment of prior authorization timeframes across payer types.
•Continue its work on encouraging payer transparency around reasons for denials by developing a clear and enforceable definition of “specific reason.” CMS should prohibit the use of vague or non-actionable denial language, so providers and their patients have adequate feedback from payers to address prior authorization claim denials.
•Continue advancing Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-based interoperability standards to improve transparency, reduce administrative burden and streamline prior authorization, while providing adequate transition time, clear technical guidance, and flexibility given current limitations in implementation and data standards.
•Modernize HIPAA prior authorization FHIR-based standards while providing adequate implementation timelines, clear guidance and transitional flexibility to avoid disrupting workflows or patient access to care.
•Finalize its proposed policy to require impacted payers to annually report standard and expedited prior authorization metrics for drugs and establish a standardized, machine readable and minimally burdensome approach.
•Advance electronic event notification for value-based care and care coordination through incentives, technical support and flexible policy levers rather than unfunded mandates.
•Work with stakeholders to strengthen healthcare cyber resilience through specific, adaptable and maturity-based standards supported by funding and operational assistance.

comment:
This comment is with regard to CMS-0062-P.
I am a biomedical researcher, patient, and patient advocate with regard to migraine and other headache disorders. I strongly support CMS’s proposal to improve prior authorization transparency and timeliness under CMS-0062-P. As a patient, I know that timely prior authorizations mean more days of life and productivity and less suffering. As a scientist, I know that treating migraine disorders sooner also reduces the probability of future disability and chronicity promoting health and saving money.
Along these lines, with regard to transparency, it would also help our community substantially if patients did not have to expend a lot of time failing medications for payer purposes that are no longer recommended as firstline therapies by professional societies. With regard to migraine therapy, this would be taking the American Headache Society’s recommendations to use anti-CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) therapeutics as first-line treatments (botox, gepants, and monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP and its receptors). It would be most helpful for payers to follow scientific evidence (see citations below) and to have to provide scientific justification when denying coverage. Along these lines another example in our field where further transparency is called for is that there is substantial evidence that different anti-CGRP therapies can work together in complementary ways (botox targeting C-fiber pain receptors and gepants and monoclonal antibodies targeting Adelta-fibers, for example). The scientific evidence (see citations below) should be used in decisions so that patients and our healthcare system can maximally benefit, which will save everyone money and time in the longrun.
In summary, I strongly support CMS’s proposed efforts to improve prior authorization transparency, interoperability, and timeliness under CMS-0062-P. Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important topic.
