title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
FR Section: II.A.2 (API requirements – denial of access)
FR Page: 19950

Source Text
“…the only reason impacted payers may deny an app or developer API access is if it would present an unacceptable level of risk to the security of PHI on the payer’s system. These risks include, for example, insufficient authentication or authorization controls, poor encryption, or reverse engineering. The payer must make that determination using objective, verifiable criteria that are applied fairly and consistently across all apps and developers.”

Proposed Comment
I appreciate the focus on strengthening cybersecurity practices and the importance of patient access to health information. I encourage consideration of implementation flexibility and clear guidance on the criteria organizations may rely on to identify an unacceptable level of security risk, so that organizations can decline access to demonstrably insecure applications with confidence that such determinations will be regarded as consistent and in good faith. I respectfully suggest that CMS consider supporting recognized application attestation or vetting approaches, such as voluntary, industry-developed code-of-conduct frameworks, and consider patient-facing transparency that clearly informs individuals when their information will be transmitted to an application that may not be subject to HIPAA protections. Recognizing the diversity of operational environments and the importance of maintaining patient safety, continuity of care, and the protection of sensitive health information, such guidance would help health care providers and payers support patient access while responsibly managing third-party and downstream cybersecurity risks.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
At the beginning of 2026, my Botox treatment for chronic migraine was denied despite having been on this therapy for approximately two years with documented benefit. Botox had become an important part of my migraine management plan and had helped reduce the severity and frequency of my attacks.

Because of the denial, my provider was required to complete a new prior authorization and appeal process, which significantly delayed my scheduled treatment. During this interruption in care, my migraine condition worsened dramatically. I ultimately developed status migrainosus, requiring hospitalization for three days due to an uncontrolled migraine attack that would not break with outpatient treatment.

This disruption in an established and effective treatment plan had a serious impact on my health and daily functioning. My symptoms became severe enough that I was unable to maintain my employment, and I ultimately lost my job while dealing with this medical crisis.

For patients with chronic migraine, delaying effective preventive treatment can have significant consequences. Botox was not a new or experimental therapy for me—it was an established treatment that was helping manage a disabling neurological condition. The delay caused by the denial and appeals process contributed to a significant decline in my health and quality of life.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
I am an independent data scientist developing an AI system that converts unstructured prior authorization (PA) policy PDFs into standardized, machine-readable representations of their clinical criteria, with deterministic validation of model outputs. I receive no funding from payers, PBMs, or manufacturers. My full comment letter is attached as a PDF; the following summarizes it.
I strongly support the proposed rule. Extending electronic PA, decision-timeframe, transparency, and API requirements to drugs addresses the most burdensome and least transparent segment of utilization management. My four comments concern one issue the rule depends on but does not directly address: the translation of payers' human-written policies into the computable artifacts the rule requires, and the fidelity of that translation.
COMMENT 1 - The policy-to-artifact translation problem (Sec. II.B.3, incorporating medical-benefit drugs into the Prior Authorization API via the Da Vinci CRD/DTR/PAS IGs). The scope is appropriate, but the binding constraint on compliance quality will be knowledge engineering, not API engineering: converting each payer's prose criteria into FHIR Questionnaire and CQL artifacts faithful to the written policy. This is currently manual and repeated at every revision. In developing an extraction system across public payer PA documents, I have observed recurring obstacles to faithful translation: logical ambiguity, where and/or step-therapy chains group ambiguously and two reasonable implementers compile materially different logic; internal inconsistency, where a parameter such as a reauthorization interval differs between a summary table and the body; and non-computable criteria expressed in irreducibly discretionary terms. These observations are preliminary, from system development rather than a completed study. Their implication is that two payers can each implement "conformant" DTR artifacts from the same policy yet adjudicate differently, reproducing in computable form the inconsistency the rule aims to eliminate. I recommend CMS acknowledge translation as a distinct compliance activity, clarify that API-exposed computable criteria should be semantically faithful to the published policy, and encourage validated, auditable translation methods including automated extraction with human verification.
COMMENT 2 - Semantic, not only structural, conformance (Sec. II.A.3, II.A.4). I support requiring the CRD, DTR, and PAS IGs, but current conformance testing verifies the structural validity of artifacts (e.g., that questionnaires use CQL for pre-population), not whether the CQL is correct with respect to the written policy. A payer could pass testing while serving logic that contradicts its own published policy, contains unsatisfiable criterion paths, or resolves ambiguity in an undisclosed way. I recommend CMS, with ASTP/ONC and tooling developers, establish an expectation that computable PA artifacts be validated for semantic equivalence with the published criteria and internal logical consistency (compiling without contradiction; no unsatisfiable paths) - initially via guidance, pilots, or voluntary certification, with potential future rulemaking. Automated methods for such checks exist. Absent this, the rule's investment risks digitizing rather than resolving existing inconsistency.
COMMENT 3 - Lag between policy changes and published machine-readable indicators (Sec. II.A.2). Responding to CMS's request for comment on update lag in Formulary & Benefit files: my work indicates PA policies are revised frequently and that human-readable criteria, machine-readable indicators, and operative logic may not be reliably synchronized or version-stamped. Undated, unversioned criteria are a structural failure point, since providers, EHR vendors, and patients cannot tell which version governs a request. I recommend CMS require PA criteria and indicators made available under the rule to carry an effective date and version identifier, and set a maximum permissible lag between a policy's effective date and its reflection in machine-readable sources.
COMMENT 4 - Public reporting and criteria transparency (Sec. II.C.7, II.C.2.c). I strongly support public reporting of drug PA metrics and the specific-reason-for-denial requirement, and recommend two additions. First, add a criteria-transparency metric: whether a payer's complete drug PA criteria are publicly retrievable without login, machine-readable, and version-dated - a low-cost, auditable measure that also lets anyone verify API-served logic matches published policy. Second, note in guidance that a denial reason is only as meaningful as the criterion it references; where criteria are contradictory or ambiguous, payers cannot reliably generate consistent reasons, reinforcing the consistency expectation above.
I would welcome the opportunity to share my research methods and results with CMS's Office of Healthcare Experience and Interoperability once it is available.

title: Comment on CMS-2026-1255-0001
comment:
Artificer Health, Inc. submits these comments on CMS-0062-P, Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs (Docket No. CMS-2026-0062). Our full signed comment is attached as a PDF.

We support the proposed rule, including its central proposal to adopt the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), and Prior Authorization Support (PAS) Implementation Guides, along with Clinical Data Exchange (CDex) for attachments, as mandatory standards under HIPAA Administrative Simplification. Our comments concentrate on four areas where agency action will materially affect clinician burden, patient access, and the safety of clinical care:

1. Preserve the treating clinician's medical-legal final authority over prior authorization submissions, in the preamble and regulatory text, without mandating any particular architecture.

2. Adopt Tier 1 mandatory Inferno conformance testing with published scores as the floor, and publish specific trigger conditions before escalating to Tier 2 and Tier 3. As of our June 12, 2026 scan of 134 payer FHIR endpoints, zero of the 73 live endpoints met full Da Vinci Prior Authorization Support conformance, seven months from the CMS-0057-F API deadline.

3. Adopt Payer-to-Payer routing of step-therapy determinations with a patient-level clinical safeguard, informed by our Chief Medical Officer's clinical experience in eating disorders, pediatric psychiatry, and obesity medicine.

4. Resolve the medical-benefit versus pharmacy-benefit drug routing problem by requiring payers to publish a machine-readable benefit-determination signal retrievable by clinician-side tools at the point of order.

We also support phased extension of prior authorization reform to laboratory tests and DMEPOS, and the October 1, 2027 compliance target. The attached PDF contains our full comment and supporting detail.

Respectfully submitted,
Bobby Kuzma, Founder and Chief Executive Officer
Nikhil P. Rao, MD, MSc, Chief Medical Officer
Artificer Health, Inc.
